# Add a Skill, Command or Agent

Skills, commands and agents are the three shared items a runtime loads on demand. This guide shows the file each one is, how to register it and how each runtime receives it.

## Skills

A skill is packaged instructions an agent loads when a task matches. Create `skills/<kebab-name>/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: write-changelog-entry
description: Draft a changelog entry from the current diff. Use when a change is ready to commit.
---

# write-changelog-entry

## steps

1. Run `git diff` to see what changed.
2. Write one line in the past tense that a user would understand.
```

`name` must equal the directory name. `description` matters most: runtimes match tasks against it, so say what the skill does and when to use it. Supporting files, such as references or scripts, sit beside `SKILL.md` in the same directory. A skill directory with no `SKILL.md` is an error unless `skills/sync-exclude.json` lists it.

## Commands

A command is a prompt a user invokes by name, as `/<kebab-name>`. Create `commands/<kebab-name>.md`:

```markdown
---
description: Run the test suite and summarize any failures.
argument-hint: "[test path or -k expression]"
allowed-tools: Bash, Read
---

Run the tests and report the result in a few plain sentences.
```

`description` is required. `argument-hint` and `allowed-tools` are optional, and a runtime that has no equivalent drops them.

## Agents

An agent is a subagent definition a session can delegate to. Create `agents/<kebab-name>.md`:

```markdown
---
name: diff-reviewer
description: Review the uncommitted changes for mistakes. Use when a change is ready.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: sonnet
---

You review a diff; you do not edit files.
```

`name` must equal the filename stem. `tools` is a comma separated list from the runtime's own tool vocabulary, and `model` is a short alias such as `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`; `stratarc validate` checks the tool names. Map the aliases to each runtime's model names with `runtime_settings.<runtime>.aliases` in `components.json`.

## Register and Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` adds a `skill:`, `command:` or `agent:` row to `control-plane.md` with the `global` column on and every project off. Put an `x` in a project's column to give that project the item as well, see [Use the Control Plane](use-the-control-plane.md). Then:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

## What Each Runtime Receives

Where a runtime reads a different format, the file is translated rather than copied.

| item | Claude Code | Codex | Gemini CLI | Cursor | OpenCode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| skill | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | not deployed | `skill/<name>/SKILL.md` |
| command | `commands/<name>.md` | `prompts/<name>.md` | `commands/<name>.toml` | not deployed | `commands/<name>.md` |
| agent | `agents/<name>.md` | `agents/<name>.toml` | `agents/<name>.md` | not deployed | `agents/<name>.md` |

[Runtimes](../reference/runtimes/README.md) has one page per runtime with the details.

# Claude

This page is the reference for what Stratarc writes into the Claude Code target, `~/.claude/` by default. Claude Code is the native format for the source, so most of this is a structured copy. The adapter is `stratarc/adapters/claude.py`.

## Target

`runtimes.claude.target` in `stratarc.toml`, default `~/.claude`. Claude Code is the one runtime `stratarc init` enables.

## Outputs

| output | built from | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md` | `AGENTS.md` with the rules digest | three identical copies |
| `settings.json`, `permissions` | `permissions.json` | the allow, deny and ask lists, `defaultMode`, `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`, and `additionalDirectories` joined with `runtimeDirectories`; `autoMode` is copied whole |
| `settings.json`, `hooks` | `hooks/hooks.json` | merged: groups that name a script Stratarc ships are replaced, groups from plugins or other tools are kept |
| `settings.json`, `enabledPlugins` | `components.json` plugins | an entry is true only when the `global` column selects it; plugins Stratarc did not enable are left as they were |
| `settings.json`, `model` and others | `runtime_settings.claude` in `components.json` | `model`, `subagent_model` and the `settings` object are passed through |
| `hooks/` | `hooks/*.sh` and `hooks/lib/` | executable bits kept |
| `skills/` | `skills/` | one directory per skill |
| `commands/` | `commands/*.md` | copied as written |
| `agents/` | `agents/*.md` | copied as written; a `model` alias is mapped through `runtime_settings.claude.aliases` |

## Not Written

User-level MCP servers live in `~/.claude.json`, outside the target, so a sync does not render them. It names each selected server in its output so nothing is dropped silently. Rules are not written as files at user scope, because the digest in `AGENTS.md` already carries them; inside a project, rules are written under `.claude/rules/`.

## Projects

A project checkout receives `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md` and `GEMINI.md` at its root, shared rules under `.claude/rules/`, skills under `.claude/skills/`, and a `settings.json` only when the project registers hooks of its own.

`notes-cli` is a command-line notes tool written in Python. Notes are stored as plain files in a directory named by the `NOTES_HOME` environment variable, with a small SQLite index beside them in `notes.db`.

## layout

- `notes_cli/`: the package. `storage.py` reads and writes notes, `search.py` queries the index, `cli.py` holds the commands.
- `tests/`: the pytest suite.
- `changelog.md`: user-facing changes, newest under `unreleased`.

## working-in-this-project

Run `python3 -m pytest -q` before proposing a commit. Never open or edit `notes.db` directly; use the commands in `notes_cli/cli.py`. A change to the on-disk format follows the `storage-format-is-versioned` rule.

The section order is shared across projects. Empty sections carry no additional project-specific instructions; project rules appear under the relevant section.

stratarc

One agent configuration source, rendered into any agent runtime you use.

Installation · Quick Start · How It Works · Commands · Docs · Contributing

--- If you use more than one coding agent, you already know the problem. Claude Code wants a `CLAUDE.md` and a `settings.json`. Codex wants `AGENTS.md`. Gemini CLI, Cursor and OpenCode each want their own layout, their own hook format and their own idea of what a rule or a skill looks like. You end up with five copies of the same instructions, and they drift apart the moment you stop paying attention. Stratarc gives you one place to write it all down. You keep a single source tree of instructions, rules, hooks, skills, commands, agents and permissions. Stratarc compiles that tree into the native format of any runtime you enable and deploys it into the right directory. Edit once, sync, and every agent receives as much of that configuration as its runtime can express. Where a runtime has no equivalent (Cursor takes no skills, commands or agents, for one), nothing is invented: the [runtimes reference](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/reference/runtimes/README.md) lists what each runtime receives and what it does not. ## Why Stratarc? | Without Stratarc | With Stratarc | | --- | --- | | Edit five config files, forget one, and the runtimes diverge | Edit one source, sync once, and every runtime gets the parts it supports | | Copy rules between runtimes and fix the formatting by hand | Write a rule once; each adapter renders the runtime's own format | | No record of what is deployed where | The control plane lists every item and the runtimes and projects it reaches | | Hand-merge project config into global settings | Project configuration is delivered from the same source tree | | Locked to the runtimes a tool ships with | Bring your own runtime with one Python file | ## Who This Is For - Developers using two or more AI coding agents who want them to behave the same way. - Teams standardizing agent configuration across members, with the source tree kept in git. - Anyone tired of copying rules between runtimes. - Anyone who wants to try a new agent without rewriting their setup. ## Highlights - **Any runtime, one source.** Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and OpenCode are all rendered from the same tree; enable the ones you use. - **Everything agents read.** Instructions, rules, hooks, skills, commands, subagents and permissions, each translated into the form the runtime expects. - **Safe by default.** `diff` and `check` show exactly what would change before `sync` writes anything, and Stratarc only ever touches files it owns. - **Validated before deploy.** The source root's hook registry and component manifest are checked against the contracts in the bundled JSON Schemas, and the rest against the engine's own rules, before every run writes anything. - **Projects too.** Managed project checkouts receive their configuration alongside the user-level runtime directories. - **Bring your own runtime.** A runtime Stratarc does not ship with is one Python file in your source root; `stratarc adapter new` writes the starting point, and it is managed like the rest. - **Nothing to install but Python.** Pure standard library at runtime, no dependencies. ## Installation Stratarc needs Python 3.11 or newer. [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/) is the easiest way to get a command-line tool onto your path: ```bash pipx install stratarc ``` Or pin a tagged release straight from GitHub, here 0.3.1, the newest release published to PyPI: ```bash pipx install git+https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc@v0.3.1 ``` The docs on the default branch describe the code there, which can be ahead of the newest release (see Unreleased in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md)); install from `git+https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc` without a tag to match them exactly. Then check the install and see which runtimes Stratarc found on your machine: ```bash stratarc doctor ``` ## Quick Start Scaffold a source root wherever you like to keep it: ```bash stratarc init ~/stratarc-source ``` Open `~/stratarc-source/stratarc.toml` and enable the runtimes you use. Then fill in the rules, skills and hooks under the same directory; every file the scaffold writes is commented, so it shows you where each piece goes. Preview what a deploy would change. `diff` is read only, so run it as often as you like: ```bash cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff ``` When the diff looks right, write it out to the enabled runtimes: ```bash cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync ``` That is the whole loop. From here on, changing your agent setup means editing one tree and running `sync`. ## How It Works A source root is an ordinary directory. This is roughly what `stratarc init` gives you: ```text stratarc-source/ ├── stratarc.toml which runtimes are enabled and where they live ├── AGENTS.md shared instructions any runtime receives ├── rules/ one Markdown file per rule, plus tiers.json ├── hooks/ hook scripts and hooks.json, the hook registry ├── skills/ one folder per skill ├── commands/ slash commands ├── agents/ subagent definitions ├── permissions.json the single permission policy ├── components.json MCP servers, plugins and other external components ├── projects/roots/ control-plane.md and per-project configuration overrides └── templates/project/ the starting point for a new project ``` A source root made by Stratarc 0.3 keeps `control-plane.md` at the top and the project overrides in `projects-root/`; the `[layout]` table in `stratarc.toml` says which a root uses. On `sync`, Stratarc validates the tree, hands it to one adapter per enabled runtime, and each adapter renders the files that runtime expects into its target directory: | Runtime | Target | Receives | | --- | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `~/.claude` | `CLAUDE.md`, `settings.json`, hooks, skills, commands, agents | | Codex | `~/.codex` | `AGENTS.md`, `config.toml`, rules, hooks, skills, prompts | | Gemini CLI | `~/.gemini` | `GEMINI.md`, `settings.json`, policies, hooks, skills | | Cursor | `~/.cursor` | rules, hooks, `hooks.json` | | OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode` | `AGENTS.md`, `opencode.jsonc`, rules, hooks, skills | The runtime directories are generated output. Change the source, run `sync`, and they are rebuilt. `sync --verify` proves that what is on disk matches what the adapters render; it does not prove that a runtime loads and enforces them. Each adapter records the newest runtime version it was tested against, and `stratarc adapter status` compares that with the version you have installed. A complete worked example lives in [examples/notes-cli](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/tree/main/examples/notes-cli): a small source root beside the exact output each runtime receives from it. ## Commands | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | | `stratarc setup` | Walks through creating a source root, choosing runtimes and the first deploy. | | `stratarc init TARGET` | Scaffolds a new source root from the bundled template. | | `stratarc doctor` | Reports the health of the install without changing anything. | | `stratarc validate` | Checks the source root's hook registry and component manifest against the bundled schema contracts, and the rest against the engine's rules. | | `stratarc diff` | Prints what a sync would change and writes nothing. | | `stratarc check` | Compares each runtime directory with the source and exits 6 when anything is stale. | | `stratarc sync` | Renders the source root into the enabled runtimes and managed projects. | | `stratarc prune` | Removes files a runtime holds that the source no longer produces. | | `stratarc reconcile` | Refreshes `control-plane.md`, the table that records which item reaches which scope. | | `stratarc projects` | Delivers each project's configuration from the project configuration directory (`projects/roots/` in a new source root) into its checkout. `sync` runs it for you. | | `stratarc gen-rules-digest` | Renders the rules digest, or embeds and checks it inside hand-authored instruction files. | | `stratarc components` | Validates `components.json` and, with `--list`, prints what it declares. | | `stratarc drift` | Reports where project checkouts differ from what the control plane delivers. | | `stratarc workflows` | Checks and shows the optional workflow module configuration. | | `stratarc adapter` | Lists the adapters, and writes the starting point for a runtime of your own. | Running `stratarc` with no arguments starts a guided setup the first time; after that it shows the status of the install and the commands to run next. `stratarc help COMMAND` shows one command's help, the same as `stratarc COMMAND --help`. Every command accepts `--help` and `--json`. The [CLI reference](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/reference/cli.md) covers the full surface, including exit statuses and the JSON envelope, and the [command reference](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/reference/generated/commands.md) lists every command and option, generated from the parser. ## Documentation The docs live in one tree under `docs/`, following the [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) layout: tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation. - **Using it:** start with [getting started](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/tutorials/getting-started.md), then browse the rest of [docs](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/README.md). - **Hacking on it:** start with [first contribution](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/docs/tutorials/first-contribution.md), which sits in the same tree. - **What ships:** the [changelog](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md). ## Contributing Contributions are welcome. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) first; it will save you a round trip. If you are stuck or have found a bug, [SUPPORT.md](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/SUPPORT.md) says where to ask and where to file an issue. ## Security Please report vulnerabilities privately as described in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/SECURITY.md) rather than opening a public issue. ## License Stratarc is released under the [MIT License](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/blob/main/LICENSE).

# Notes CLI

A worked example of stratarc from the first command to the last. It is small enough to read in ten minutes and complete enough that every directory the engine reads holds a real entry.

## The Scenario

You maintain `notes-cli`, a command-line notes tool written in Python. You use Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and OpenCode, and you were tired of keeping five configurations in step by hand. So you keep one source root, `~/stratarc-source`, and let stratarc render it into all five.

Three things matter to you, and they are what the example configures:

- No agent ever commits your notes database. A global rule says so and a hook enforces it on shell commands.
- Commit messages follow one style everywhere, and you have one skill, one command and one agent you use in every project.
- `notes-cli` itself has stricter needs: its own instructions, a rule about the on-disk format, a rule that tests use a temporary directory, and a tighter permission policy.

The example has three parts. `source/` is the source root you would write, `expected/` is the output a sync of it produces, and this page connects the two.

## The Source Root

Everything under `source/`. A file marked "no row" is read directly by the engine as configuration and has no line in `control-plane.md`; every other file has one.

| file | why it exists | control-plane row |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stratarc.toml` | Enables all five runtimes, names their target directories, and names the projects root that holds the checkouts. | linked from the runtime rows |
| `AGENTS.md` | The instructions every agent reads. It carries a marker pair where the rules digest is written. | `instruction-file` |
| `permissions.json` | The single permission policy, in Claude Code rule syntax, that each runtime adapter translates into its own enforcement. | no row |
| `components.json` | The manifest of external components. This example declares none. | no row |
| `control-plane.md` | The inventory that decides which resource reaches which scope. | not applicable |
| `rules/tiers.json` | Assigns each rule file to the `global`, `common` or `project` tier. | no row |
| `rules/never-commit-local-databases.md` | A `global` rule: applies everywhere and cannot be opted out. | `rules` |
| `rules/conventional-commit-messages.md` | A `common` rule: applies to every scope by default. | `rules` |
| `rules/tests-use-a-temporary-directory.md` | A `project` rule: applies only where a project opts in, here `notes-cli`. | `rules` |
| `hooks/hooks.json` | Registers the one hook on `PreToolUse` for shell commands. | no row |
| `hooks/block-database-commits.sh` | The hook script. It refuses a `git add` or `git commit` that names a database file. | `hooks-pre-tool-use` |
| `skills/write-changelog-entry/SKILL.md` | A skill that drafts a changelog line from the current diff. | `skills` |
| `commands/test-summary.md` | The `/test-summary` command: run the tests and summarize failures. | `commands` |
| `agents/diff-reviewer.md` | A read-only subagent that reviews a diff. | `agents` |
| `projects-root/notes-cli/AGENTS.md` | Instructions for the `notes-cli` checkout only. | `project-local-configuration` |
| `projects-root/notes-cli/rules/storage-format-is-versioned.md` | A rule that exists only for `notes-cli`. | `project-local-configuration` |

Each JSON file validates against the schema shipped under `stratarc/data/schema/`, and `tests/test_examples.py` checks that along with the shape of every rule and skill.

## The Managed Project

Every checkout under `projects_root` is a managed project. Here that is `~/projects/active/notes-cli`, a checkout in the `active/` status folder. It appears as a column in every table of `control-plane.md`, and `projects-root/notes-cli/` holds what is true of that project alone.

| concern | top level | `projects-root/notes-cli/` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instructions | `AGENTS.md` is deployed to each runtime directory. | `AGENTS.md` is deployed into the checkout, as `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md` and `GEMINI.md`. |
| Rules | The digest holds the `global` and `common` rules. | The digest also holds the `project` rule the column opts into, and `.claude/rules/` receives the shared rules plus the project-local one. |
| Shared rules in the checkout | Not applicable. | A rule the global scope already ships arrives as its binding section only, so a session does not read it twice. A rule only this project uses, and the project-local rule, arrive whole. |
| Skills | Deployed to each runtime's skills directory. | The shared skill the column opts into lands in `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/`, which the runtimes read per project. |
| Hooks, commands, agents | Deployed at user scope. | Not overridden, so the user scope versions apply. |

The result for a session in `~/projects/active/notes-cli` is the shared baseline plus the three project additions, with nothing to copy by hand.

## Walkthrough

Every command below runs today. Run each from the directory shown.

### 1. Initialize

```bash
cd ~ && stratarc init ~/stratarc-source
```

```text
stratarc init: wrote 11 files to /home/you/stratarc-source
```

That scaffold is a bare source root: the instruction file, the configuration, an empty control plane and a README in each directory. Fill it in, or take the finished example. This copies it over the scaffold, from the root of your stratarc checkout:

```bash
cd <your stratarc checkout> && cp -R examples/notes-cli/source/. ~/stratarc-source/
```

### 2. Edit a Rule

You decide `perf` deserves its own commit type. Edit `~/stratarc-source/rules/conventional-commit-messages.md`, in the source root and nowhere else:

```diff
-Write each commit subject as `type(scope): summary`, using `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test` or `chore` as the type.
+Write each commit subject as `type(scope): summary`, using `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test` or `chore` as the type.
```

Nothing deployed has changed yet. Runtime directories are generated output and are only rewritten by `sync`.

### 3. Check

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc check
```

`check` compares what each runtime directory holds with what the source would render, changes nothing, and lists every file that is out of date. After step 2 that is every file that carries the digest, because the changed rule is `common` and reaches every scope:

```text
claude/AGENTS.md  claude/CLAUDE.md  claude/CODEX.md
codex/AGENTS.md   gemini/GEMINI.md  opencode/AGENTS.md
notes-cli/AGENTS.md  notes-cli/CLAUDE.md  notes-cli/CODEX.md  notes-cli/GEMINI.md
notes-cli/.claude/rules/conventional-commit-messages.md
```

That listing is illustrative; run the command for the real output.

### 4. Diff

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

`diff` shows the change itself, file by file, without writing it. For `claude/AGENTS.md` it is the one line you edited, rendered into the digest:

```diff
-Write each commit subject as `type(scope): summary`, using `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test` or `chore` as the type. Keep the summary lowercase, imperative and under 72 characters. Put the reason for the change in the body, not the subject.
+Write each commit subject as `type(scope): summary`, using `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test` or `chore` as the type. Keep the summary lowercase, imperative and under 72 characters. Put the reason for the change in the body, not the subject.
```

That diff is illustrative too; run the command for the real output.

### 5. Sync

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

`sync` renders the source into each enabled runtime and into the managed project. It writes only the files it owns and leaves everything else in a runtime directory alone, so settings you keep by hand survive. Its output names each file it writes. The result is what `expected/` holds. The hook registration for Claude Code, for example, lands in `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
"hooks": {
  "PreToolUse": [
    {
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [
        {
          "type": "command",
          "command": "$HOME/.claude/hooks/block-database-commits.sh",
          "timeout": 3
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### 6. What Appears Under Each Runtime

The same source becomes five different layouts, because each runtime reads its own formats.

```text
~/.claude/                       Claude Code
  AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md CODEX.md   AGENTS.md plus the rules digest, three identical copies
  settings.json                  permissions.json and hooks/hooks.json
  hooks/block-database-commits.sh
  skills/write-changelog-entry/SKILL.md
```

### 7. Reconcile

You add a command. Create `~/stratarc-source/commands/release-checklist.md` with a `description` in its frontmatter and a short prompt as the body, then run:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` notices the new source file, adds a row for it to `control-plane.md`, and leaves every existing cell as you set it. A new command opts in globally and stays off for the project until you choose it:

```text
| [command:release-checklist](commands/release-checklist.md) | x |  |
```

Run `stratarc sync` and the command appears in `~/.claude/commands/`, `~/.codex/prompts/`, `~/.gemini/commands/` and `~/.config/opencode/commands/`.

### 8. Prune

You decide the command was a mistake and delete `~/stratarc-source/commands/release-checklist.md`. Reconcile removes its row:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

A sync adds and updates but does not delete, so the four deployed copies are still there. `prune` removes the files in a runtime directory that the source no longer produces:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc prune
```

It touches only paths stratarc owns, such as `commands/` and `prompts/`, so a command you installed into a runtime by hand stays.

# Expected

The rendered runtime output a sync of `../source` produces, one directory per runtime plus `project/notes-cli/` for the managed project. The source root lives at `~/stratarc-source` and the checkout at `~/projects/active/notes-cli`. `tests/test_examples.py` runs `stratarc sync` on a copy of `../source` in a temporary home and requires every file here to match the output byte for byte.

`<home>` in `codex/config.toml` stands for the home directory the sync ran under, which the engine writes into the project trust table.

A sync also writes files that are not kept here: the packaged hook libraries under `hooks/lib/`, the project's `.docs/` snapshot of the control plane, the OpenCode plugin `plugins/stratarc-hooks.ts`, and the per-target `.stratarc-deploy.json` and `stratarc-delivered.json` stamps. They come from the engine's package data or record times and absolute paths, and the test lists them in `ENGINE_OWNED`.

# schema

`hooks.schema.json` validates `hooks/hooks.json`, the canonical hook registry: each of the eight canonical events maps to a list of hook groups, each group carries an optional tool `matcher` and a non-empty list of command hooks with an optional timeout in seconds. The `hook-registry` check in `stratarc/validate.py` enforces the same contract with the standard library on every `validate`, `sync`, `check` and `diff`, and the tests hold the two in agreement.

`permissions.schema.json` validates `permissions.json`, the single permission policy every adapter translates: `schemaVersion` 1, the `allow`, `deny` and `ask` rule lists, the writable runtime directories, the Codex approval policy, network and shell environment settings, and the auto-mode guidance block. Unknown top-level keys are accepted, matching the engine's loader.

`components.schema.json` validates `components.json`, the manifest of external components: MCP servers, plugins, foreign hook groups, third-party skills and dependencies, plus per-runtime settings. Checks that need code, such as unique entry names and the token-shaped value scan, are listed in the schema's `$comment`.

# agents

Agents are subagent definitions a session can delegate a task to. Each agent is one Markdown file `agents/<kebab-name>.md` with YAML frontmatter carrying `name` (equal to the filename stem), `description` (when to delegate to it) and, optionally, `tools` (a comma separated tool list) and `model` (a runtime alias such as `opus`, `sonnet` or `haiku`), followed by a Markdown body that is the agent's system prompt.

# commands

Commands are prompts a user invokes by name, as `/<kebab-name>`. Each command is one Markdown file `commands/<kebab-name>.md` with YAML frontmatter carrying a `description` and, optionally, `argument-hint` (the arguments shown to the user) and `allowed-tools` (a comma separated tool list), followed by a Markdown body that is the prompt the agent runs.

# Hooks

Hooks are scripts a runtime runs when something happens in a session, such as before a tool call. `hooks.json` is the registry: it maps a canonical event name (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart` or `SubagentStop`) to a list of groups, each with an optional `matcher` (a tool name pattern) and a list of `{"type": "command", "command": "$HOME/.claude/hooks/<script>.sh", "timeout": <seconds>}` entries. The script itself is `hooks/<kebab-name>.sh`. `stratarc sync` copies each selected script into the runtime and rewrites the registration into that runtime's own format; a runtime with no equivalent for an event drops it and says so.

# rules

Rules are standing instructions every agent session follows. Each rule is one Markdown file named `<kebab-name>.md`, with no frontmatter, an H1 equal to the filename stem, and a `## binding` section holding the short normative text that `stratarc sync` renders into the rules digest of each runtime's instruction file; any further sections (rationale, examples, exceptions) stay in the full file, which the digest links to. A rule is rendered only once `rules/tiers.json` lists its filename under a tier: `global` rules apply everywhere and cannot be opted out, `common` rules apply globally by default, and `project` rules apply only where a project opts in through the control plane.

# skills

Skills are packaged instructions an agent loads when a task matches them. Each skill is a directory `skills/<kebab-name>/` holding a `SKILL.md` whose YAML frontmatter carries `name` (equal to the directory name) and `description` (what the skill does and when to use it, since runtimes match tasks against this text), followed by a Markdown body with the instructions; supporting files such as references or scripts sit beside `SKILL.md` in the same directory.

# projects/roots

Project-local configuration lives here, one directory per project named exactly like the project's checkout under `projects_root` (for example `projects/roots/my-app/`). A project directory mirrors the source root's own layout for the pieces that apply only to that project: an `AGENTS.md` with project instructions, and optionally `rules/`, `skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/` and `hooks/hooks.json` in the same formats used at the top level; `stratarc sync` deploys them into that project's checkout.

# project

Scaffolding for a new project. It is part of the framework that becomes the stratarc 0.4.0 init default: nothing in it names a person, a machine or a path, and `<source-root>` stands for the path of this source root. A project has two halves: its configuration source in this repo under `projects/roots/<project>/`, and its checkout under `~/projects/active/<project>/`, which receives generated instruction files and agent config from that source.

## steps

Steps 1, 3 and 4 below are automated: run `stratarc projects --new <project>` (add `--remote <owner>/<repo>`, `--checkout <path>`, `--public` for a public repository, `--workflows` for the optional `workflows.toml` template; add `--check` to preview). It is safe to repeat, copies this folder's templates from your own source root, never overwrites a file, never delivers configuration into the checkout, and ends by checking the project. `stratarc projects --registry-check` verifies the control plane, the root folders and the registries agree. The manual steps remain as the description of what it does.

1. Copy `templates/project/roots/` to `projects/roots/<project>/` and replace every `<project>` in its `AGENTS.md`. Fill in the sections from `project-context` on and leave any that do not apply empty; keep `source-and-sync`, `session-start` and `authority-order` as they are.
2. Add the project's own skills, agents, commands, rules or hooks under `projects/roots/<project>/skills/`, `agents/`, `commands/`, `rules/` and `hooks/` only when it has them. Shared content stays in the root `skills/` and `rules/`.
3. Copy `templates/project/checkout/.gitignore` into the new checkout, and `templates/project/checkout/local/` too when you add one (the bundled template ships none, since `local/` is never committed). The `.gitignore` applies the visibility model and keeps the generated instruction files out of the project's git.
4. Register the project: add its row to the projects table and its column to the deployment tables in `projects/roots/control-plane.md`, and its GitHub slug to `projects/roots/remotes.json`. A public repository also goes in `projects/roots/public-targets.json`, which keeps all private configuration out of it.
5. Preview with `stratarc diff --root "<source-root>"`, then deploy with `stratarc sync` when the operator asks.
6. Optional drift checks. Run `stratarc drift` to compare every checkout against the control plane. If the project keeps instruction files below its root, list them under `"nested"` in `projects/roots/<project>/surfaces.json`. To check the repository in its own CI, copy `templates/project/checkout/.github/workflows/agent-drift.yml` into the checkout. A finding that is intentional is waived in `projects/roots/drift-waivers.json` with a reason and an expiry date. The optional workflow module is off by default; to enable it for this project, copy `templates/project/roots/workflows.toml` to `projects/roots/<project>/workflows.toml`, edit it, and run `stratarc workflows check`.

## generated-in-the-checkout

`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md` and `GEMINI.md` at the checkout root, and the project's agent config under the runtime folders (`.claude/`, `.agents/`, `.codex/`, `.cursor/`, `.gemini/`). Edit the source in `projects/roots/<project>/`, never these copies.

All notable changes to this project are documented in this file. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## Unreleased

### Added

- A `[layout]` table in `stratarc.toml` names the source root's project configuration directory (`project_config_dir`), control plane file (`control_plane`) and each project's internal work product folder (`local_dir`). `control_plane_managed = false` marks a hand maintained control plane that reconcile leaves alone. Defaults keep the 0.3 layout.

### Changed

- The rules digest rewrites `../` links in a rule so they resolve from the document that embeds the digest, and the source graph reads digest headings only inside the digest markers.

- Releases publish through PyPI trusted publishing from a tag-triggered workflow, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, with every action pinned to a commit and every tool installed from a hash pinned lock file. No PyPI token is used. The cut-a-release guide describes the one-time setup.

### Fixed

- `validate`, and with it the gate before every `sync`, `check` and `diff`, holds `hooks/hooks.json` to `hooks.schema.json` (new `hook-registry` check): an unknown event, a group without hooks, a hook whose type is not `command`, an empty command or a timeout that is not a number greater than 0 is refused with its event, group and hook index, never its command.
- A runtime whose installed version cannot be detected is no longer deployed silently when its adapter declares a supported range: `sync` warns once with `msg-1156` that the range was not checked, and the new `sync --strict-versions` refuses it with exit 5.
- `diff` on a source root whose control plane is stale previews against the control plane `sync` would reconcile, kept in memory, so a fresh scaffold's preview names the instruction files the deploy replaces (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, for one) instead of omitting them.
- `stratarc projects --new NAME` copies the optional `workflows.toml` only with `--workflows`, also from `templates/project/roots/`, where the bundled template keeps it, and in a projects root with no status folders it works on the checkout at `NAME` rather than `active/NAME`.
- `public-targets.json` is read from the source root's project configuration directory (`layout.project_config_dir`), where `stratarc projects --new NAME --public` writes it, and from the 0.3 location `projects-root/` as well. In a source root scaffolded with the `projects/roots` layout the list was ignored, so a checkout listed as public still received a control plane column, a snapshot and delivered configuration.
- A write run checks every runtime (hook mappings, adapter, deploy stamp, adapter version, target writability) before writing to any of them, so a predictable failure writes nothing. A failure found during the write is reported as a target by target account (`changed`, `current`, `failed`, `not-attempted`) and recorded in `~/.stratarc/state/deploy-last.json` as `complete`, `failed`, `partial`, `restored` or `restore-failed`; with `--rollback-on-drift` the runtimes already written are restored, and a restoration that cannot complete exits 5.
- A verify report (from `sync --verify`) lists the expected, compared, verified, drifted, skipped and excluded runtimes and projects with reasons, and its result distinguishes `incomplete` and `no-targets` from `verified`, so zero installed runtimes no longer reads as a successful verification. Exit statuses are unchanged; the new `sync --require-complete` exits 5 unless every expected target was compared and matched. Each report states that it shows file consistency, not runtime behavior.
- Project skill delivery no longer overwrites a file a project edited after delivery, keeps the original delivery hash so the file stays protected, and keeps legacy manifest entries that have no hash.
- Project delivery refuses a symlinked `.claude`, `.agents` or delivery manifest, and skill delivery, pruning and `--verify` no longer follow a symlink at or above a skill path.
- `prune` deletes a file in an owned directory only when the new deploy ledger (`~/.stratarc/state/deployed.json`, written by every sync) records that Stratarc deployed it, so a command, prompt or agent made by hand is reported as `unmanaged` and kept. The dry run names the evidence for each removal, and a real prune copies every deleted file to `~/.stratarc/backups/prune/` first.
- OpenCode hooks at a nondefault target run that target's registry and scripts: the bridge reads the registry beside the plugins directory it was installed into, the registry names the target's hooks directory (shell-quoted, so a path with spaces works), and a missing or malformed registry is reported on stderr instead of silently running nothing.
- The OpenCode bridge checks an `apply_patch` call once per affected file, move destinations and deletions included, with the operation and the whole patch in each payload, so a hook denying a second or deleted file blocks the call. A patch it cannot read blocks instead of being checked in part.

- A sync adds and updates files and never deletes; `prune` removes what the source no longer produces.

# Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

- Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
- Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
- Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
- Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
- Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

- The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
- Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
- Public or private harassment
- Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
- Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement through a private report on GitHub: open a security advisory at <https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/security/advisories/new> and title it "Conduct report". All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

# Contributing

Thank you for helping improve Stratarc. Open an issue to discuss a change before writing a large pull request, so the effort goes where it will be merged. This page holds the rules every contribution follows; the walkthroughs and reference live under [docs](docs/README.md), starting with [First Contribution](docs/tutorials/first-contribution.md). Everyone taking part is expected to follow the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## Setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc ~/stratarc && cd ~/stratarc && python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[test]'
```

## Tests

Run the suite before every commit. The slow marker builds a wheel and installs it into a fresh virtual environment. [Run the Tests](docs/how-to-guides/run-the-tests.md) covers the other checks.

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m 'not slow'
```

## Guidelines

- Python 3.11 or newer, standard library only at runtime. `pytest` and `jsonschema` are test dependencies.
- Runtime assets live under `stratarc/data/` and are read through `importlib.resources`, never through a path built from `__file__`. See [Package Data](docs/reference/package-data.md).
- Tests read fixtures only: never the live home directory or a user's real runtime configuration.
- A user-facing error is added to the catalog in `stratarc/messages.py` first and raised by id. After changing a command, an option or a message, run `python3 scripts/docs/generate-reference.py` and commit the regenerated pages.
- Documentation goes in `docs/`, in the folder for its kind: `tutorials/`, `how-to-guides/`, `reference/` or `explanation/`. Headings use Title Case, and each paragraph and list item is one line, not hard-wrapped.
- Never commit a secret, credential, private key or `.env` file. `.env.example` with placeholder values is allowed.
- Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/).

## Pull Requests

Keep each pull request to one change, describe what it does and how you tested it, and make sure the test suite passes. Add a line under Unreleased in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for any user-visible change. A change that affects a decision recorded under [docs/explanation/decisions](docs/explanation/decisions/README.md) should add a record that amends or replaces it.

# Security Policy

## Reporting a Vulnerability

Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub security advisories: open the repository's Security tab and choose "Report a vulnerability", or go to <https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/security/advisories/new>. Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion for a suspected vulnerability.

Include the affected version or commit, the steps to reproduce, and the impact you observed. You will receive an acknowledgement, and the fix and disclosure are coordinated with you through the advisory.

## Scope

- The `stratarc` command and the Python package.
- The hook libraries shipped under `stratarc/data/`, including any way to leak a secret past the token-shaped value detector.
- The scaffold template and the files Stratarc writes into runtime directories, including any way to make it write outside the directories `permissions.json` allows.

Vulnerabilities in the agent runtimes themselves are out of scope; report those to their maintainers. How Stratarc treats secrets and what it trusts is described in the [Security Model](docs/explanation/security-model.md).

## Supported Versions

Only the latest release and the `main` branch receive security fixes.

# Support

This page says where to get help with Stratarc and where to file what. Stratarc is maintained in the open on GitHub and has no paid or private support channel; every question and report goes through the repository, where it is visible to the next person with the same problem.

## Before You Ask

- Match your symptom against [Troubleshooting](docs/how-to-guides/troubleshooting.md).
- Check the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for what has shipped.
- Search the existing [issues](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/issues), open and closed.

## Where to File

| what you have | where it goes |
| --- | --- |
| a bug: Stratarc did something other than what the documentation says | a [bug report](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/issues/new?template=bug-report.yml) with the command you ran, what you expected, what happened and the output of `stratarc --version` |
| a question about using Stratarc | a [question](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/issues/new?template=question.yml) with what you are trying to do and what you tried |
| a request for a feature or a new runtime | a [feature request](https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc/issues/new?template=feature-request.yml) describing the need before any code; see [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) |
| a suspected security vulnerability | a private report as described in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md); never a public issue |
| a mistake or gap in the documentation | an issue, or a pull request against the page; the [docs index](docs/README.md) shows where a page goes |

## What to Include

Paste command output as text inside a code fence rather than as a screenshot, and remove anything shaped like a credential before posting. If the problem involves a source root, say which files are in it, and do not attach a `permissions.json` or `components.json` that names services you want kept private. `stratarc doctor --report` writes a redacted bundle you can attach.

## Response Times

The project is maintained by one person alongside other work. Issues are read within a few days; fixes land as time allows and in order of impact.
