# Architecture

This page explains how Stratarc turns one source root into a configuration for each enabled runtime, for a contributor who needs the shape of the pipeline before changing a stage of it. The [source layout](../reference/source-layout.md) describes the input; the [runtimes](../reference/runtimes/README.md) pages describe the outputs.

## The Idea

Every agent runtime wants the same few things in its own words: standing instructions, permissions, hooks, skills, commands and agents. Maintained by hand, five runtimes drift apart. Stratarc keeps one source root, a directory you put in git, and treats each runtime directory as generated output. Nothing in the runtime directories is authoritative, which is why a sync may overwrite what it owns.

## The Stages

1. Read and validate. Load `stratarc.toml`, resolve the registry of adapters, and run the validator over the source root. A sync stops here on an error.
2. Reconcile. Refresh `control-plane.md`, the table of which item reaches which scope, and re-embed the rules digest in `AGENTS.md`.
3. Stage. For each scope, build a staging directory that holds only the items the control plane selects: the instruction file, the selected rules, hooks, skills, commands and agents, the permission policy, and the MCP servers and plugins chosen. The whole output of the user-level scope exists before any of it is deployed.
4. Render. For each enabled runtime whose directory exists, call the adapter with the staging directory and the target. An adapter translates the staged tree into the runtime's native files and returns one line per change. In `check`, `diff` and `--verify` it is called in dry-run mode, which writes nothing.
5. Write. A real sync lets the adapters write, stamps each target with the policy version it deployed, and then delivers the active projects.

`prune` runs the reverse pass instead: it asks each adapter which directories it owns, lists what those directories hold that the current source does not produce, and removes it.

## The Pieces

- Adapters, one per runtime, in `stratarc/adapters/`, plus the ones a source root adds. They share helpers for copying with the executable bit, mirroring a directory, merging JSON and TOML without disturbing keys they do not own, and tracking what they own. See [Adapter Files](../reference/adapter-files.md).
- The registry, `stratarc/registry.py`, which holds a manifest for each adapter: the runtime versions it supports, the newest it was tested on and any deprecation. A deploy through an adapter that does not support the installed runtime stops before writing.
- The control plane, `stratarc/control_plane.py` and `stratarc/reconcile.py`. Reconcile owns the inventory and the defaults; the `x` cells belong to the user and are never overwritten.
- Staging, `stratarc/staging.py`, which makes the per-scope trees and renders the `${STRATARC_SOURCE}` token in rule pointers into a real path.
- The deploy stamp, `stratarc/deploy_guard.py`, which refuses to write an older permission policy over a newer one.
- The home, `~/.stratarc`, for backups, logs and registered manifests, written through one function that keeps a copy of anything it replaces.

## What Is Deliberately Not Here

Stratarc does not launch agents, resolve secrets, run a server or schedule anything. It reads a directory and writes directories. Anything outside that, such as a tool that injects a secret at launch, belongs to a runtime or to your own scripts, which is why configuration refers to secrets by name only. See the [Security Model](security-model.md).

# Security Model

This page explains what Stratarc protects against and how, for a reader deciding whether to trust it with their runtime configuration. It says why each protection exists and what it does not cover. To report a vulnerability, follow [Security](../../SECURITY.md).

## What Stratarc Trusts

The source root is trusted input. Stratarc renders what it finds there, and a source root can run Python of its own: adapters in `adapters/`, validator checks and project renderers in `scripts/private/`. Loading one is a decision made by whoever owns that directory, so keep it in a repository you control and review it as code.

The runtime directories are output Stratarc owns in part. It writes only the files it produces, merges into shared settings files without removing keys it does not own, and never deletes anything on a sync. Deleting is `prune`, which removes only what an adapter says it owns and lists first with `--dry-run`.

## Where It Will Write

A sync writes into a runtime directory only when that directory is listed in `runtimeDirectories` in `permissions.json` and already exists. A target that is missing from the list is refused, so a mistyped `target` in `stratarc.toml` cannot send files somewhere unexpected. Writes into `~/.stratarc` use mode 0700 and 0600, copy the file they replace into `backups/` first and replace it atomically. A file written by a newer Stratarc is never rewritten by an older one.

## Secrets

Stratarc never reads, stores or resolves a secret. Configuration refers to one by name, as `secret://namespace/key`, and whatever resolves that name at launch is outside Stratarc. Three checks keep a literal out of the files it handles:

- `components.json` refuses a value that looks like a credential, and its message names the entry and key but never repeats the value. The detector matches private key blocks, cloud and source host tokens, `sk`-prefixed API keys, JWTs, bearer tokens and long values assigned to a name containing `key`, `token` or `secret`.
- `check` reports a literal secret found in a runtime's own files, by file and key, never by value.
- The change log stores digests rather than content, and every text value passes the same detector before it is written. If the detector cannot run, the value is replaced and nothing unredacted is written.

A server whose environment uses a `secret://` reference is not rendered into a runtime file, because writing the reference would only give the runtime a string it cannot resolve. The sync output names it.

## Protection Against a Stale Source

Each runtime directory carries a stamp recording the policy version, source checkout and commit that wrote it. A deploy that would replace a newer policy version with an older one is refused. This stops a stale checkout from silently reverting a permission change, which is the failure that is easiest to miss.

## Public Repositories

A repository listed in `public-targets.json` in the project configuration directory (`projects/roots/` in a new source root, `projects-root/` in a 0.3 one) receives nothing: no delivered file, no control-plane column and no permission rewrite. A list that exists but cannot be read stops the run instead of being treated as empty, because reading it as empty would treat the one checkout the file protects as an ordinary project.

## What Stratarc Does Not Cover

It does not sandbox the runtimes. The permission policy is translated into each runtime's own enforcement, and how well a runtime enforces it is the runtime's responsibility. It does not inspect the content of hook scripts, skills or commands you write. And it does not make a runtime directory safe to share: the files it writes are readable by whoever can read your home directory.

# Add a Hook

A hook is a script a runtime runs when something happens in a session, such as before a tool call. You write the script once and register it once, and Stratarc deploys it into every runtime that has a hook system, translated to that runtime's format.

## Write the Script

Create `hooks/<kebab-name>.sh` in the source root and make it executable. The runtime sends the event payload as JSON on standard input. For a `PreToolUse` hook, exit 2 blocks the tool call and returns whatever you wrote to standard error to the agent; exit 0 allows it.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Refuse a git add or git commit that names a local database file.
set -euo pipefail

payload="$(cat)"

if printf '%s' "$payload" | grep -Eq 'git +(add|commit).*\.(db|sqlite3?)'; then
  printf 'refusing to stage a local database file\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi

exit 0
```

```bash
chmod +x ~/stratarc-source/hooks/block-database-commits.sh
```

## Register It

Add the script to `hooks/hooks.json`, which maps a canonical event to groups of hooks:

```json
{
  "PreToolUse": [
    {
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [
        {
          "type": "command",
          "command": "$HOME/.claude/hooks/block-database-commits.sh",
          "timeout": 3
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

- The event is one of `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart` or `SubagentStop`.
- `matcher` is a tool name pattern and is optional. Leave it out to match every tool.
- `command` always names the Claude Code location, `$HOME/.claude/hooks/<script>`. Each adapter rewrites the path for its runtime.
- `type` is always `command`, and `command` is a non-empty string.
- `timeout` is in seconds, greater than 0, and optional. Adapters convert it to the runtime's own unit.
- `validate`, and therefore every `sync`, `check` and `diff`, refuses a registry that breaks these rules (the `hook-registry` check) and names the event, group and hook index of each problem, before anything is written.

## Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` adds a `hook:block-database-commits` row to `control-plane.md` under the event's table, on for `global` and off for projects. Then:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

## What Each Runtime Does With It

| runtime | where the registration goes | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `hooks` in `settings.json` | the native format |
| Codex | `hooks.json` | the path points into `~/.codex/hooks` |
| Gemini CLI | `hooks` in `settings.json` | events are renamed, for example `PreToolUse` becomes `BeforeTool`, and timeouts become milliseconds |
| Cursor | `hooks.json` | entries are flat, and a matcher naming `Bash` becomes `Shell` |
| OpenCode | `hooks/hooks.json` | a small plugin that Stratarc deploys reads this registry and runs the commands |

An event a runtime cannot express is dropped, and the sync output says so. Hooks that were already in a runtime's settings and that Stratarc does not own are left in place.

## Shared Helpers

When a sync deploys hooks it also copies a small library to `hooks/lib/` in each runtime: `guard-utils.sh` holds the token-shaped value detector, `secret-scan.sh` scans text with it, and `log.sh` is a logging helper. A script of yours can `source` them from `$HOME/.claude/hooks/lib/` (the path is rewritten per runtime), and your own files in `hooks/lib/` are copied beside them.

## Test a Hook Without a Runtime

Feed the script a payload by hand:

```bash
printf '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git add notes.db"}}' | ~/stratarc-source/hooks/block-database-commits.sh; echo "exit $?"
```

# Add a Rule

A rule is a standing instruction every agent session follows. This guide shows how to write one, choose who it applies to and get it into your runtimes. Rules are rendered into a digest inside each runtime's instruction file, and the full text stays in your source root.

## Write the File

Create `rules/<kebab-name>.md` in the source root. The file has no frontmatter, an H1 equal to the filename stem and a `## binding` section:

```markdown
# keep-answers-short

## binding

Keep answers under five sentences unless the user asks for more.

## rationale

Long answers bury the decision. Any further sections stay in this file, which the digest links to.
```

The `## binding` section is the short normative text that lands in the digest. Keep it under 120 words; `stratarc validate` reports a longer one as an error. Everything after it is for readers of the file.

## Choose the Tier

List the filename under a tier in `rules/tiers.json`:

```json
{
  "global": [],
  "common": ["keep-answers-short.md"],
  "project": []
}
```

| tier | applies |
| --- | --- |
| `global` | everywhere, and cannot be opted out of |
| `common` | everywhere by default, and a project can opt out in the control plane |
| `project` | only where a project opts in |

A rule that is in no tier is not rendered anywhere.

## Register and Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` adds a `rule:keep-answers-short` row to `control-plane.md`. Then preview and deploy:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

`sync` refreshes the digest block in `AGENTS.md` (between the `BEGIN RULES-DIGEST` and `END RULES-DIGEST` markers, which you never edit) and copies it into each runtime's instruction file.

## Make a Rule Apply to One Project

Put the rule in the `project` tier, then open `control-plane.md` and put an `x` in that project's column on the rule's row. See [Use the Control Plane](use-the-control-plane.md). A project can also carry rules of its own that no other project sees: [Set Up a Project](set-up-a-project.md).

## Check It Landed

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc check
```

`check` exits 0 when every runtime matches the source and 6 when something is out of date.

# Add a Runtime

Stratarc ships adapters for five runtimes. If you use another agent tool, you add it yourself: a runtime is one Python file in your source root, and it is managed by the same commands as the others. This guide builds one from the generated starting point.

## Generate the Starting Point

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc adapter new acme-agent --target .acme-agent
```

This writes `adapters/acme-agent.py` and adds `~/.acme-agent` to `runtimeDirectories` in `permissions.json`, the list of directories a sync may write into. `--target` is the runtime's directory under your home; leave it out and it defaults to `.<name>`. The name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, and must not be one of the five that ship.

The generated adapter already works: it copies `AGENTS.md` into the runtime's directory. Create the directory and try it:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.acme-agent && cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --only acme-agent
```

The control plane gains a `runtime:acme-agent` row on the next `reconcile` or `sync`, and `stratarc.toml` needs no entry unless you want a different `target` or `enabled = false`.

## The File Contract

An adapter file has a literal `RUNTIME` dict and two functions. [Adapter Files](../reference/adapter-files.md) is the full reference; this is the shape:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from stratarc.adapters._common import OwnedDir

RUNTIME = {
    "name": "acme-agent",
    "target": ".acme-agent",
    "hook_registry": None,
    "hook_events": ["PreToolUse", "PostToolUse", "PostToolUseFailure", "Stop",
                    "UserPromptSubmit", "SessionStart", "SubagentStart", "SubagentStop"],
}


def sync(source: Path, target: Path, dry_run: bool = False) -> list[str]:
    ...


def owned_outputs(source: Path, target: Path) -> list[OwnedDir]:
    ...
```

`source` is the staged output for the user-level scope: `AGENTS.md`, `rules/`, `skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `hooks/` and `permissions.json`, holding only the items the control plane selected. `target` is the runtime directory. `sync` writes what the runtime needs and returns one line per change it makes, or would make when `dry_run` is true. It must write nothing when `dry_run` is true.

## Translate More of the Source

Edit `sync` to render the other kinds. Look at a shipped adapter for the format work: `stratarc/adapters/gemini.py` turns commands into TOML and renames hook events, `stratarc/adapters/opencode.py` writes a permission object. Helpers in `stratarc.adapters._common` copy files while preserving the executable bit and mirror a directory, deleting nothing unless asked.

## Tell Stratarc What You Own

`owned_outputs` returns the directories your adapter fills and the names it puts there. `check` uses it to tell a file you wrote from one the runtime or the user put there, and `prune` removes only files in an owned directory that the source no longer produces:

```python
def owned_outputs(source, target):
    commands = frozenset(p.name for p in (source / "commands").glob("*.md"))
    return [OwnedDir("command", target / "commands", commands)]
```

## Declare the Hook Events

`hook_events` lists every canonical event your adapter handles, and a deliberate drop counts. A sync refuses to run a runtime that is missing an event your `hooks/hooks.json` registers, so list all eight even if you drop some.

## Keep It Honest

- `stratarc validate --strict` fails if `stratarc.toml` has a `[runtimes.<name>]` table with no adapter.
- `stratarc diff --only acme-agent` and `stratarc check --only acme-agent` give you the same preview and drift report as the shipped runtimes.
- A test for your adapter can call `sync` against a temporary directory, as `tests/test_runtime_extension.py` in the Stratarc repository does.

An adapter file runs Python from your source root during every sync, so treat the source root like code you trust.

# Configure Runtimes

This guide shows how to choose which runtimes receive your configuration, move a runtime's target directory, and keep a runtime out of a sync. A runtime is any agent tool Stratarc has an adapter for: the five that ship with it, plus any you add in [Add a Runtime](add-a-runtime.md).

## See What Is Available

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --list
```

The list names every runtime, its target directory and whether that directory exists. A sync writes only into a target that exists, so a runtime you have not installed is skipped without an error.

## Enable or Disable a Runtime

Each runtime has a table in `stratarc.toml`:

```toml
[runtimes.claude]
enabled = true
target = "~/.claude"

[runtimes.codex]
enabled = false
target = "~/.codex"
```

`enabled = false` keeps the runtime out of `sync`, `check`, `diff` and `prune`. A runtime with no table at all is treated as enabled, as long as its target exists. A table for a runtime that has no adapter is an error, not a silent skip: `stratarc sync` stops and `stratarc validate --strict` exits 1, naming the missing adapter file.

## Move a Target

Set `target` to the directory the runtime reads its configuration from. `~` expands to your home directory.

```toml
[runtimes.opencode]
enabled = true
target = "~/dotfiles/opencode"
```

A target must also appear in `runtimeDirectories` in `permissions.json`, the list of directories a sync may write into. A sync refuses a target that is missing from it and names the runtime:

```json
{
  "runtimeDirectories": ["~/.claude", "~/dotfiles/opencode"]
}
```

## Deploy to One Runtime

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --only codex
```

`--only` also works with `check`, `diff` and `prune`. It skips project delivery, so it is a quick way to try a single adapter.

## Choose Per Scope in the Control Plane

The control plane has a `runtime:<name>` row for each runtime. The `global` column decides whether the runtime receives anything at all; an empty cell skips it the way `enabled = false` does. See [Use the Control Plane](use-the-control-plane.md).

## Try a Runtime Against a Scratch Home

Point `--home` at an empty directory to see exactly what a runtime would receive, without touching your real directories:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && mkdir -p /tmp/try/.codex && stratarc --home /tmp/try sync --only codex
```

Then look in `/tmp/try/.codex`. [Runtimes](../reference/runtimes/README.md) lists what each one receives.

# Cut a Release

This guide is for a maintainer releasing a new version of Stratarc: bumping the version, settling the changelog and pushing the tag that publishes the package. Publishing runs in `.github/workflows/release.yml` through PyPI trusted publishing, so no PyPI token exists anywhere to leak. It assumes a clean checkout of `main` with the test suite green.

## Where the Version Lives

The version is `__version__` in `stratarc/__init__.py`. `pyproject.toml` declares the version as dynamic and reads it from that file through hatchling, so it is set in one place. The project follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## One-Time Setup

These steps are done once, by the repository owner, before the first release that uses the workflow.

1. On pypi.org, open the `stratarc` project, then Publishing, and add a trusted publisher: owner `klappe-pm`, repository `stratarc`, workflow `release.yml`, environment `pypi`.
2. In the repository settings, create an environment named `pypi` with yourself as a required reviewer, a deployment rule that allows only tags matching `v*`, and administrator bypass turned off.
3. Add a tag ruleset for `v*` so that only maintainers can create, move or delete release tags.

## Steps

1. Decide the new version from the Unreleased section of [the changelog](../../CHANGELOG.md): a breaking change bumps the major version, a new capability bumps the minor, a fix bumps the patch. A version number that was ever uploaded to PyPI can never be reused, even after it is deleted.
2. Set `__version__` in `stratarc/__init__.py`.
3. In the changelog, rename Unreleased to the version and the date, and open a new empty Unreleased section above it.
4. Run the full test suite, including the slow wheel test:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && python3 -P -m pytest
```

5. Commit as `chore: release <version>` and merge it through a pull request like any other change.
6. Tag the merge commit `v<version>` and push the tag:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && git tag -a v<version> -m "stratarc <version>" && git push origin v<version>
```

7. The release workflow starts on the tag. Its build job refuses a tag that is not on `main` or does not match `__version__`, builds the distributions with hash pinned tools and records their checksums in the job summary. Its test job installs the built wheel and runs the suite against it. Its publish job waits for your approval in the `pypi` environment; approve it once the first two jobs are green.
8. Create a GitHub release on the tag with the changelog section as its notes.

The project page shows the README, so every link in it must be absolute, and the page text of a published version can never be changed; a fix ships as a new version.

## The Lock Files

`requirements/build.txt` and `requirements/ci.txt` pin every tool the workflow installs, with hashes. They are compiled from `requirements/build.in` and `requirements/ci.in`. To update them, edit the `.in` file and recompile:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && python3 -m pip install pip-tools && pip-compile --generate-hashes --strip-extras --output-file=requirements/ci.txt requirements/ci.in
```

## After the Release

Confirm that `pipx install stratarc==<version>` works, that `stratarc init` scaffolds a source root, and that the project page on pypi.org renders the README with working links.

# Install

This guide covers installing Stratarc: the supported methods, the Python versions it runs on, and how to upgrade and uninstall. If you have never used Stratarc, [Getting Started](../tutorials/getting-started.md) walks the install as one step among several.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer. Stratarc has no runtime dependencies beyond the standard library.

## Install from PyPI

```bash
pipx install stratarc
```

`pipx` keeps the command in its own environment and puts it on your path. Plain `pip install stratarc` works too, into whichever environment is active.

## Install from the Repository

To install straight from GitHub, for example a tagged release, name the tag after an `@`:

```bash
pipx install git+https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc@<tag>
```

Leave off the `@<tag>` to follow the default branch.

## Which Version These Docs Describe

PyPI carries the newest published release, and each tagged release on GitHub has a matching entry in [CHANGELOG.md](../../CHANGELOG.md). These docs, on the default branch, describe the code on the default branch, which can be ahead of PyPI: its changes are listed under Unreleased in the changelog, and `stratarc --version` reports the version it is being prepared as. To run exactly what the docs describe, install from the repository without a tag. Where a released version behaves differently, the page says so; the main difference today is the source root layout `stratarc init` writes, described in [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

## Install for Development

Contributors install an editable copy with the test dependencies. See [First Contribution](../tutorials/first-contribution.md) for the full setup.

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[test]'
```

## Check the Install

```bash
stratarc --version
```

```bash
stratarc doctor
```

`doctor` reports the Python version, the home directory, the source root it resolved and each runtime with its target directory. It exits 3 when the home directory cannot be written to and 2 when the source root or its `stratarc.toml` is unusable, and says which.

## Upgrade

```bash
pipx upgrade stratarc
```

For a repository install, run `pipx reinstall stratarc` to pick up the latest commit.

## Uninstall

```bash
pipx uninstall stratarc
```

Uninstalling removes the command only. Your source root, the `~/.stratarc` home and anything already deployed into runtime directories stay where they are.

# Migrate Existing Config

You already have runtime directories you maintain by hand: a `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, some commands, a hook or two, MCP servers. This guide moves that into one source root without losing what you have, in an order that lets you check each step before anything is overwritten.

## Start from a Scaffold

```bash
stratarc init ~/stratarc-source
```

Put the directory in git before you start. Everything below is a normal edit you can review and undo.

## Move the Instructions

Copy the contents of your main instruction file (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` or similar) into `~/stratarc-source/AGENTS.md`, above the `RULES-DIGEST` markers. Leave the markers alone; `sync` fills the block between them. Split standing instructions that should be followed everywhere into rules, one file each: [Add a Rule](../how-to-guides/add-a-rule.md).

## Move Commands, Agents, Skills and Hooks

Copy each file into the matching source directory, in the format described in [Add a Skill, Command or Agent](add-a-skill-command-or-agent.md) and [Add a Hook](add-a-hook.md). A command or agent file written for one runtime usually works as is for Claude Code, and Stratarc translates it for the others. Register hook scripts in `hooks/hooks.json`.

## Move Permissions

`permissions.json` holds one policy in Claude Code's rule syntax, which every adapter translates into its runtime's own enforcement. Copy your `allow`, `deny` and `ask` lists in, and list every runtime directory you deploy to under `runtimeDirectories`.

## Declare What Other Tools Installed

MCP servers, plugins, hook groups and skills that another tool installs are not yours to author, but Stratarc should know about them so it does not treat them as strays. List them in `components.json`: an `mcp_servers` entry per server, a `plugins` entry per plugin, a `foreign_hooks` entry with a `match` for each hook group another tool registers, and a `third_party_skills` entry for each skill directory it installs. Reference secrets as `secret://namespace/key`, never as values; Stratarc refuses a token-shaped literal.

## Check Before You Write

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc validate --strict
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

`validate` catches a misspelled tool name, a bad registry entry or a rule with no binding section. `diff` shows every change to every runtime, against the control plane as `sync` will reconcile it, and writes nothing. Read it for what the first deploy replaces:

- A `would copy` line names a file the source produces, such as `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or a command with the same name as yours. The deploy replaces that file whole, so its content must already be in the source.
- `render permissions.json into ~/.claude/settings.json` replaces the runtime's whole permission block (`permissions` in Claude Code, `permission` in OpenCode, and so on) with the policy in `permissions.json`. Every other key in the file stays.

Then:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc check
```

`check` lists what each runtime holds that your source does not own, under headings such as unmanaged, undeclared and foreign hook group. Each line is either something to move into the source, something to declare in `components.json`, or something to leave alone. A file under `unmanaged` was never deployed by Stratarc, so `prune` never deletes it.

## Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --verify --rollback-on-drift
```

The first deploy writes only files the source produces and merges into your settings files without removing entries it does not own. With `--rollback-on-drift` it first copies every runtime file it will change into `~/.stratarc/backups/`, and puts the runtime directories back if the result does not match or a runtime fails partway; the copies stay there either way, so a file you meant to keep can be recovered by hand, as [Roll Back a Deploy](roll-back-a-deploy.md) describes. From here on, edit the source and not the runtime directory: a later sync overwrites a hand edit to a file Stratarc owns.

# Preview and Deploy

Stratarc separates looking from writing. `diff` and `check` never write; `sync` writes. This guide shows how to see a change before it lands, deploy it, and keep a runtime directory free of files the source no longer produces.

## See What Would Change

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

`diff` renders the source exactly as a sync would and prints each file it would copy, merge or write, with paths shown under `~`. It writes nothing and exits 0 even when it finds differences. It also reports a rule you added since the last sync, because it re-embeds the rules digest in a scratch copy instead of reading the stale one.

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc check
```

`check` makes the same comparison and exits 6 when anything is out of date. It also reports what each runtime holds that the source does not own: orphan files (deployed by an earlier `sync`, no longer produced), unmanaged files (never recorded as deployed, left alone), hook groups another tool registered, and literal secrets found in a runtime's files. Use it in a script or a pre-push step.

## Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

Before it writes, `sync` validates the source and stops on an error. It then refreshes `control-plane.md` and the rules digest, and renders each enabled runtime whose directory exists, and each active project. It writes only files it owns, merges into shared settings files without disturbing your own entries, and never removes a file. A line per change names what it did.

To try one runtime, or a dry run that is the same as `diff`:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --only gemini
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --dry-run
```

## Remove What the Source No Longer Produces

`sync` adds and updates but does not delete. After you delete a rule, command or skill from the source, its deployed copy is still in each runtime. List what would go, then remove it:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc prune --dry-run
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc prune
```

`prune` removes only paths in directories Stratarc owns, such as `commands/`, `prompts/`, `agents/` and `rules/`, and only files the current source does not produce and an earlier `sync` recorded deploying. Every write run adds what it rendered to the deploy ledger, `~/.stratarc/state/deployed.json`; a file the ledger never recorded is unmanaged, so a command you installed into a runtime by hand stays, and `prune --dry-run` names it under `unmanaged` beside each removal and the evidence for it. A rule named in `rules/retired.json`, a hook registration whose script is missing, and a component `components.json` declares `wanted: false` are removed on that evidence instead.

Before deleting anything, `prune` appends the list to `~/.stratarc/telemetry/prune-<date>.txt` and copies each file it deletes to `~/.stratarc/backups/prune/<run time>/<runtime>/`, under its path inside the runtime's target. To recover a file, copy it back from there. A home written by a release before the ledger existed has recorded nothing, so `prune` keeps every such file until a `sync` has run; delete a file the source dropped before then by hand.

## Verify After the Write

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --verify
```

`--verify` re-renders after the write and compares byte for byte with what is on disk. It exits 6 on a difference. See [Roll Back a Deploy](roll-back-a-deploy.md) for restoring automatically.

## Read the Exit Status

| status | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | done, or nothing to do |
| 2 | the source is invalid, or a guard refused the deploy |
| 5 | an adapter does not support the installed runtime version |
| 6 | `check` or `--verify` found drift |

The full table is in [CLI](../reference/cli.md), and each message id is explained in [Errors](../reference/generated/errors.md).

# Roll Back a Deploy

A sync that exits 0 says only that the writes did not fail. This guide shows how to confirm that what is deployed equals what the source describes, how to have Stratarc undo a deploy that does not match, and what protects you from deploying an older policy over a newer one.

## Verify Instead of Trusting

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --verify
```

After writing, `--verify` renders again into a scratch area and compares it with the deployed files byte for byte. Drift means exactly what a dry run would change. It never writes a deployed file, and it exits 6 when it finds drift.

The report lists every target it covers: the runtimes and projects it expected, the ones it compared, verified or found drifted, and the ones it skipped, each with a reason. A runtime `stratarc.toml` enables but that is not installed is expected and skipped; one that is turned off, or neither installed nor named, is excluded and listed with its reason. The result is `verified` only when every expected target was compared and matched, `incomplete` when an expected target was skipped, `no-targets` when nothing was compared and `drift` on any difference. The JSON report carries the same lists under `coverage` and a `complete` flag. Only drift changes the exit status, as before; to make automation require full coverage, add `--require-complete`, which exits 5 (message `msg-1155`) unless the result is `verified`:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --require-complete
```

A clean result is evidence of file consistency only: the same adapters render what is on disk. It does not show that a runtime loaded those files or enforces them; every report says so in its `evidence` field.

## Roll Back Automatically

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --verify --rollback-on-drift
```

Before it writes, the run backs up every file each adapter will change, and each runtime's deploy stamp. If verification finds drift, it puts the backups back, removes files the run created and exits 6. If a backup is missing it exits 5 and names the file, instead of reporting a restore it cannot perform.

Rollback covers the runtime directories only. Project checkouts are verified but never rolled back, because they are working trees that may hold edits of yours. The three flags (`--verify`, `--rollback-on-drift`, `--require-complete`) cannot be combined with `--only`, `--check`, `--diff`, `--dry-run`, `--prune` or `--list`.

## When a Deploy Fails Partway

Before writing anything to a runtime or project, a write run checks every enabled runtime: each hook event has a mapping, the adapter is present and supports the installed version, the deploy is not older than the one in place, and the target can be written. If any check fails, nothing is written to any runtime or project, and the run exits 2 (5 when the only failure is an unsupported adapter version). The run does refresh the source root's derived files first, the rules digest in `AGENTS.md` and `control-plane.md`, which a later run regenerates.

A failure only the write can find, such as a runtime file the component renderer refuses to rewrite or a write the system rejects, fails that runtime; the others still deploy, and project delivery is not attempted. The run then prints a `sync: deployment:` account naming every target as `changed`, `current`, `failed` or `not-attempted`, with the reason, and exits with the failure's status. Every write run also writes the account to `~/.stratarc/state/deploy-last.json`, whose `result` is `complete`, `failed` (nothing was written), `partial` (something was), `restored` or `restore-failed`.

With `--rollback-on-drift`, a partial deployment puts back the runtime files it wrote from the backups taken before the write, and the account marks those runtimes `restored`; the exit status is still the failure's. If a backup is missing, the runtimes are marked `restore-failed` and the run exits 5. Restoration rewrites only the files the run backed up or created, so an unrelated file you edited in the meantime is left alone, and running the same command again is safe. Project checkouts and the source root are never rolled back.

## Restore a File by Hand

Every file Stratarc replaces in its own home, and every runtime file a `--rollback-on-drift` run changes, is first copied into `~/.stratarc/backups/`. Look there for an older copy:

```bash
ls ~/.stratarc/backups
```

## Clean Up Old Backups

Backups grow until you clean them. This lists what would go and removes nothing:

```bash
stratarc doctor --clean
```

Add `--yes` to remove it. The clean keeps the newest 20 versions of each file and anything under 30 days old, and never touches your settings or registered adapters.

## The Stale-Source Guard

Each runtime directory receives a stamp file, `.stratarc-deploy.json`, recording the policy version, the source checkout and its commit. A deploy that would replace a newer policy version with an older one is refused with a message naming both versions and the checkout that wrote the newer one. This protects you when several checkouts or machines share a runtime directory. Bump `policyVersion` in `permissions.json` when you change the policy.

# Run the Tests

This guide covers running the test suite: the markers, the slow wheel test, the worked example and the two checks that need `bash` and `bun`. It assumes the editable install from [First Contribution](../tutorials/first-contribution.md).

## The Test Suite

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

Tests live under `tests/` and read only fixtures under `tests/fixtures/`, never a real home directory or real runtime configuration. A full run takes about a minute.

## The Slow Marker

One test is marked `slow`: it builds a wheel from the checkout, installs it into a fresh virtual environment, and runs the installed `stratarc` outside the checkout. It scaffolds a source root and compares it with the bundled template byte for byte, runs a dry-run sync and `doctor` against a temporary `HOME`, then adds a runtime of its own with `adapter new` and syncs it. It proves that the package data and the adapters ship correctly; see [Package Data](../reference/package-data.md). Skip it while iterating and run it before you commit:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m 'not slow'
```

## The Worked Example

`tests/test_examples.py` runs `stratarc diff`, `sync` and `check` on a copy of `examples/notes-cli/source` in a temporary home and compares what `sync` wrote with `examples/notes-cli/expected`, byte for byte. In the expected files `<home>` stands for the temporary home path. A sync also writes per-target stamp files and a few generated files that `expected/` does not hold; the `ENGINE_OWNED` pattern in the test lists them. When an adapter changes what a sync writes, the test names the files that differ. Update them from the output of a sync in a throwaway home, as the [example](../../examples/notes-cli/README.md) describes.

## The Shell and Bun Tests

Tests under `tests/` named `*.test.sh` run with `bash` and are marked `shell`; a non-zero exit fails them. The OpenCode hook bridge test, `tests/hooks/opencode-runtime-hooks.test.ts`, runs with `bun test` and is marked `bun`. It is skipped when `bun` is not installed, as are the tests in `tests/test_adapters_opencode.py` that load an installed bridge with `bun` to prove a nondefault OpenCode target runs its own hooks. Run only one kind with `-m shell` or `-m bun`.

## The Reference Pages

Two pages under `docs/reference/generated/` are written from the code. A test fails when either differs from what the code produces. After changing a command, an option or a message, regenerate them:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python scripts/docs/generate-reference.py
```

# Set Up a Project

Most of your configuration is user-wide. This guide shows how to give one project checkout its own instructions and rules, choose which shared items reach it, and keep a project out of the way. Stratarc calls the project-specific part the project-local configuration, and it lives in `projects/roots/<project>/` in your source root. The paths in this guide are the layout `stratarc init` writes; a source root made by Stratarc 0.3 uses `projects-root/<project>/` and a top-level `control-plane.md` instead, as the `[layout]` table in [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md) describes.

## Tell Stratarc Where Your Projects Are

Set `projects_root` in `stratarc.toml` to the directory that holds your checkouts:

```toml
projects_root = "~/code"
```

Every directory under it that has a `.git` entry is a project. The checkouts can sit directly in that directory (a flat layout), or inside status folders named `active`, `new`, `inactive`, `archived` and `external`. In a flat layout every checkout is active. With status folders, only `active` projects receive configuration, so moving a project to `archived/` stops delivery to it. A checkout can also sit one grouping folder down, such as `~/code/work/api`. The default is `~/projects`. You can override it for one command with `--projects-root`.

## Add Project-Local Files

Let Stratarc create the project folder from `templates/project/` in your source root, named exactly like the checkout. Preview first, then create it:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc projects --new notes-cli --dry-run
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc projects --new notes-cli
```

`--new` copies `templates/project/roots/` to `projects/roots/notes-cli/`, adds the project to the control plane, and, when the checkout exists, adds its `.gitignore` block. It never overwrites a file and never delivers configuration into the checkout. `--remote owner/repo` records the GitHub slug and `--checkout PATH` names a checkout outside the projects root. To do it by hand instead, create the folder yourself:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/stratarc-source/projects/roots/notes-cli/rules
```

It mirrors the source root's own layout for the pieces that apply to that project only:

| path | holds |
| --- | --- |
| `projects/roots/<project>/AGENTS.md` | the project's instructions |
| `projects/roots/<project>/rules/` | rules only this project follows |
| `projects/roots/<project>/skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/` | items only this project has |
| `projects/roots/<project>/hooks/hooks.json` | hooks for this project |

Rules follow the same format as top-level rules: an H1 equal to the filename stem and a `## binding` section.

## Choose What Else Reaches the Project

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` finds the checkout and gives the project a column in every table of `projects/roots/control-plane.md`. A shared skill, command or agent starts off in a project's column, and a rule follows its tier: `global` and `common` rules are on, `project` rules are off. Put an `x` in a cell to opt the project in to a shared item, or clear it to opt out of a `common` rule. See [Use the Control Plane](use-the-control-plane.md).

## Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc projects --check
```

`sync` renders the user-level runtimes and then every active project. Inside a project it writes `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CODEX.md` and `GEMINI.md` at the checkout root, rules and skills under `.claude/`, and skills under `.agents/`. Rules the user-level instructions already carry arrive as their binding section only, so a session does not read them twice. `projects --check` reports files that disagree with what delivery would write.

## Narrow a Project's Permissions

A project can carry its own `permissions.json` with a `projectScope` key that names the exact checkout and any worktrees it applies to:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "policyVersion": 1,
  "defaultMode": "default",
  "projectScope": {
    "root": "/home/you/code/notes-cli",
    "worktrees": []
  },
  "allow": ["Read(/home/you/code/notes-cli/**)", "Edit(/home/you/code/notes-cli/**)"],
  "deny": ["Read(**/notes.db)"],
  "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"]
}
```

Paths must be absolute, the root's final component must be the project name, and the file cannot grant extra shared directories or bypass approvals. Shared denials still apply. `stratarc sync` rewrites the runtime permission files a project already has, such as `.claude/settings.json`, so they state this policy; it never creates one for an ordinary project.

## Keep a Repository Out

Some repositories should receive nothing, for example one you publish. List them in `projects/roots/public-targets.json` (`projects-root/public-targets.json` in a 0.3 source root), by directory name or `owner/repo`. `stratarc projects --new NAME --public` adds a new project there for you:

```json
{
  "targets": ["my-published-tool", "someone/their-repo"]
}
```

A listed checkout, or a linked worktree of one, gets no control-plane column, no delivered files and no permission rewrites. A file that exists but cannot be read stops the run instead of being treated as empty.

# Troubleshooting

This guide matches a message or a symptom to its fix. Every refusal prints a message id of the form `msg-NNNN` and exits with a status from the exit-code map; look the id up in [Errors](../reference/generated/errors.md) for the full problem and recovery. If your problem is not here, see [Support](../../SUPPORT.md).

## `stratarc doctor` First

```bash
stratarc doctor
```

It reports the Python version, the home directory and whether it can be written, the source root it resolved and how (`--root`, `STRATARC_SOURCE`, the nearest `stratarc.toml`, or the current directory), and each runtime with its target and whether that exists. Most problems below show up there.

## Init Refuses the Target

`stratarc init` writes only into a directory that does not exist or is empty, and says `exists and is not empty` otherwise. Pick a new directory, or empty the one you named. It never merges a template into existing files.

## A Runtime Is Skipped

A sync writes only into a runtime whose target directory exists, and skips the rest without an error. Check `stratarc sync --list`. Run the runtime once so it creates its directory, or set `target` in `stratarc.toml`. A runtime with `enabled = false`, or an empty `runtime:<name>` cell in the `global` column of the control plane, is skipped too.

## Missing `runtimeDirectories` Entry

```text
sync: claude: missing runtimeDirectories entry for ~/.claude
```

A sync writes only into directories `permissions.json` lists under `runtimeDirectories`. Add the target, using `~` for your home. `stratarc adapter new` does this for a runtime you add.

## A Runtime Table Has No Adapter

`[runtimes.<name>]` in `stratarc.toml` names a runtime that no adapter provides, and `sync` stops. Either remove the table, or create `adapters/<name>.py` in the source root: [Add a Runtime](add-a-runtime.md).

## Refusing to Deploy: Validation Found an Error

```text
sync: refusing to deploy; stratarc.validate --strict --checks generic found an error
```

Run the validator to see the findings, which name the file and the problem:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc validate --strict
```

Common ones are an agent whose `tools` line names a tool the runtime does not have, a rule with no `## binding` section or one over 120 words, an entry in `components.json` with an unknown key, and a hook registered in `hooks/hooks.json` whose script does not exist.

## A New Rule or Item Does Not Appear

`diff` and `sync` read `control-plane.md`. After you add a source file, run `stratarc reconcile` (a sync does this first). A rule must also be listed in a tier in `rules/tiers.json`, and its `x` must be on in the scope's column. The message `control-plane: stale` means a row is missing or out of date, and `reconcile` fixes it.

## A Deployed File Keeps Reverting

A sync overwrites any file Stratarc owns, so a hand edit to a deployed `AGENTS.md`, command or rule is lost on the next sync. Edit the source instead. Settings files such as `settings.json` are merged, so keys Stratarc does not own are kept.

## A Newer Policy Is Already Deployed

```text
deployed policy version 7 (from /path/to/other-checkout) is newer than the source's version 5; refusing to write an older policy over it
```

Another checkout deployed a higher `policyVersion` to the same runtime directory. Update this checkout from the other one, or raise `policyVersion` in `permissions.json` if this change is the newer one.

## Components Refuse a Token

`components.json` accepts secrets only as `secret://namespace/key` references. A value that looks like a credential is refused, and the message names the entry and key but never repeats the value. Replace it with a reference, and rotate the credential if it was ever committed.

## An Adapter Does Not Support the Installed Runtime

`msg-1114` (exit 5) means the runtime version is outside the range the adapter supports, so the deploy stops before writing. `msg-1115` is a warning that the runtime is newer than the version the adapter was tested against, and the deploy continues. `msg-1156` is a warning that the runtime's version could not be detected (its command is not on `PATH`, or did not answer), so the adapter's declared range was not checked; the deploy continues, and `stratarc sync --strict-versions` refuses it with exit 5 instead. `stratarc adapter status` compares every adapter with its installed runtime.

## The Check Exits 6

`stratarc check` exits 6 when a runtime differs from what the source renders. Run `stratarc diff` to see each file. If the difference is a hand edit you want to keep, move it into the source; if it is not, `stratarc sync` replaces it.

## The Home Cannot Be Written

Exit 3 with `msg-1003` or `msg-1118` means `~/.stratarc` is missing or not writable. Make it writable, or point at another home with `--home` or `STRATARC_HOME`.

# Use the Control Plane

The control plane is `control-plane.md` in your source root, at `projects/roots/control-plane.md` in one `stratarc init` writes (at the top in a 0.3 source root; `layout.control_plane` in `stratarc.toml` names it). It is a set of tables that records, for every item you author, which scope it reaches: the user-level runtimes (the `global` column) and each project. This guide shows how to read it, how to change what reaches where, and how to keep it current. The file format is in [Control Plane](../reference/control-plane.md).

## Read It

Each table is one kind of item, one row per item, one column per scope:

```markdown
## commands

| option | global | notes-cli |
|---|---|---|
| [command:test-summary](commands/test-summary.md) | x |  |
| [command:release-checklist](commands/release-checklist.md) | x | x |
```

An `x` means the item is on for that scope. Anything else, including an empty cell, means it is off. Here `/test-summary` is deployed to the user-level runtimes only, and `/release-checklist` also reaches the `notes-cli` project. The first cell of a row links to the source file.

## Change What Reaches Where

Edit a cell and save. The `x` marks are the one part of the file you edit by hand.

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

Clearing the `x` in a project's column removes that item from the project on the next sync, and clearing it in the `global` column removes it from the user-level runtimes. `diff` shows the removal before it happens.

## Keep It Current

Run `reconcile` after you add, rename or delete a source file or project:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

Reconcile adds a row for each new item with its default, drops the row of a deleted one, adds a column for a project it found and keeps every `x` you set. Defaults: a new skill, command, agent or hook is on for `global` and off for projects, and a rule follows its tier. `stratarc sync` runs the same step first, so a sync never works from a stale table. `stratarc reconcile --check` reports whether the file is stale without writing, and exits 6 if it is.

## Choose a Runtime Per Scope

The `runtimes` table has a `runtime:<name>` row for each adapter, including ones you added yourself. Clearing the `global` cell of a runtime keeps it out of the sync without touching `stratarc.toml`.

## Add a Project Column

A project gets a column when it has a checkout under your projects root and is not listed in `public-targets.json`. See [Set Up a Project](set-up-a-project.md). Each active project also receives a generated copy of its own column as `local/stratarc-control-plane.md` (the folder `layout.local_dir` names, `.docs/` when unset), a record of what the project was given. Do not edit it.

## What Not to Do

Do not add rows by hand. A row you type has no source file behind it, and the next reconcile removes it.

# Adapter Files

An adapter translates the staged source into one runtime's native files. Five ship in the package, and a source root adds its own in `adapters/<name>.py`. Both kinds use the same file contract, described here. For a walkthrough, see [Add a Runtime](../how-to-guides/add-a-runtime.md).

## Where They Are Found

The registry reads the packaged adapters, then every `*.py` file in the source root's `adapters/` directory whose name does not start with an underscore or end in `.test.py`. The directory is considered only when the source root has a `stratarc.toml`. A source adapter that reuses the name of a packaged runtime is refused.

The registry reads the `RUNTIME` constant of each file with `ast.literal_eval`, without importing it, so listing runtimes costs no import. A file whose `RUNTIME` is missing or malformed stops the command with a message naming the file. Sync imports a source adapter by file path when it needs it.

## RUNTIME

A module-level dict literal:

| key | type | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | the runtime name; must equal the file name without `.py`, and is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens |
| `target` | string | the runtime's directory relative to the home, such as `.claude` or `.config/opencode`; no leading `/` or `~`, no `..` |
| `hook_registry` | string or `None` | the file under the target that holds hook registrations, such as `settings.json`, or `None` when the runtime has no JSON registry |
| `hook_events` | list of strings | the canonical hook events the adapter handles, a deliberate drop included |

Any other key is an error. A sync refuses a runtime that is missing an event the staged `hooks/hooks.json` registers.

## Sync

```python
def sync(source: Path, target: Path, dry_run: bool = False) -> list[str]:
```

`source` is the staged tree for the user-level scope. It holds only what the control plane selected, laid out as the source root is: `AGENTS.md`, `rules/` (with `tiers.json`), `hooks/` (with `hooks.json` rewritten for the claude path prefix and `lib/`), `skills/`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `permissions.json`, and `components.json` reduced to the selected MCP servers and plugins. `target` is the runtime directory.

The function writes what the runtime needs and returns one human-readable line per change. When `dry_run` is true it must write nothing and return the lines it would have produced, because `diff`, `check`, `--verify` and rollback all depend on that. It should be idempotent: a second run on an unchanged tree returns no lines.

Helpers in `stratarc.adapters._common` copy a file while keeping the executable bit, mirror a directory without deleting extra files by default, and rewrite the Claude hook path prefix for a runtime. The shipped adapters are the reference for format work.

## Owned_outputs

```python
def owned_outputs(source: Path, target: Path) -> list[OwnedDir]:
```

Returns the target directories the adapter owns and the names it puts in them, computed the same way `sync` computes them. `OwnedDir(kind, path, names)` takes a label such as `"command"`, the absolute directory and the set of file names (or, for per-item directories such as skills, directory names). `check` reports anything else in an owned directory as an orphan when the deploy ledger records that an earlier write run put it there, and `prune` deletes it; anything else there is unmanaged, reported and left in place. Every write run records the names this function returns that exist on disk. A function that returns `[]` owns nothing, and `check` then reports nothing about the runtime's directories.

## Optional: External_inventory

An adapter may also define `external_inventory(target)` returning a list of `Item` records describing what the runtime holds that the source does not own: MCP servers, plugins, skills, foreign hook groups. `check` and `prune` use it to report items as declared, undeclared or returned against `components.json`. See `stratarc/adapters/_inventory.py` for the record type.

## Manifests

Each adapter also has a manifest used for version support: the runtime versions it supports, the newest one it was tested on, and a deprecation record. The packaged adapters carry theirs in `stratarc/adapters/_supports.py`, and a source adapter gets a permissive one derived from its file. `stratarc adapter register` stores a stricter manifest under `~/.stratarc/adapters/<name>/manifest.json`, and `stratarc adapter status` compares every manifest with the installed runtime. A manifest never adds a runtime; only an adapter file does.

# CLI

This page describes how the `stratarc` command behaves as a whole: how it finds your source root, what the global options do, the JSON output and the exit statuses. Every command and option is listed in the generated [Commands](generated/commands.md) page, and every message in [Errors](generated/errors.md). For when to use a command, see the [how-to guides](../how-to-guides/README.md).

## Running Stratarc with No Command

`stratarc` on its own adapts to where it runs. In a terminal with no source root found, it starts `stratarc setup`. In a terminal with a source root found, it prints where the source root is, which runtimes are enabled and the commands to run next, and exits 0. A root named by `--root` or `STRATARC_SOURCE` is used as given and never starts setup; one that does not exist is refused with `msg-1001`. Outside a terminal it prints the help and exits 0, so a script never waits on a prompt. With `--json` it is invalid input (`msg-1011`) and exits 2.

## Commands

| command | does |
| --- | --- |
| `help [COMMAND]` | lists every command, or explains one with examples; `stratarc help sync` is the same as `stratarc sync --help` |
| `setup` | walks through creating or adopting a source root, choosing runtimes from those installed, previewing the first deploy and deploying on an explicit yes; records the source root in `~/.stratarc/config.toml`; needs a terminal |
| `init TARGET` | writes a new source root from the bundled template into an absent or empty directory |
| `doctor` | reports the health of the install, the home and the source root; `--permissions`, `--clean` and `--report` extend it |
| `sync` | renders the source into every enabled runtime and managed project |
| `check` | reports what is out of date, writes nothing and exits 6 on drift |
| `diff` | prints what a sync would change, writes nothing and exits 0 |
| `prune` | deletes files a runtime holds that the source no longer produces |
| `reconcile` | refreshes `control-plane.md` from the source tree |
| `validate` | checks a source root against the schemas and the engine's rules |
| `projects` | delivers the project configuration directory (`layout.project_config_dir`) into the managed project checkouts |
| `gen-rules-digest` | renders or checks the rules digest in instruction files |
| `components` | validates `components.json` and lists what it declares |
| `drift` | reports where checkouts differ from what the control plane delivers, writes nothing to them and exits 6 on drift |
| `workflows` | checks and shows the optional workflow module configuration, in the control plane `[workflows]` table and each project's `workflows.toml`, and exits 1 on a problem |
| `adapter` | lists, shows, creates, registers and deprecates adapters |

## Global Options

Global options are accepted before or after the command, and each lasts for that one command.

| option | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--root PATH` | the source root; sets `STRATARC_SOURCE` |
| `--home PATH` | the home every runtime target and `~` hangs under; sets `STRATARC_HOME` |
| `--projects-root PATH` | the directory that holds project checkouts; sets `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR` |
| `--json` | print one JSON envelope instead of text |
| `--debug` | print a traceback when a command stops unexpectedly |
| `--version` | print `stratarc <version>` and exit 0 |
| `--help` | print the usage summary, a short start here list and the exit statuses, and exit 0 |

## How the Source Root Is Found

In order: `--root`, the `STRATARC_SOURCE` environment variable, the nearest directory at or above the current one that holds `stratarc.toml`, the source root `stratarc setup` recorded in `~/.stratarc/config.toml` when it still holds `stratarc.toml`, and the current directory. A command that reads the source refuses the current directory when it holds no `stratarc.toml` (`msg-1009`), so running `stratarc sync` in the wrong directory writes nothing. `stratarc doctor` prints which of these decided. The home is `STRATARC_HOME`, then `HOME`. The projects root is `--projects-root`, then `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR`, then `projects_root` in `stratarc.toml`, then `~/projects`. See [Configuration](configuration.md).

## The JSON Envelope

With `--json` a command prints exactly one object on standard output and exits with the same status as without it.

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "data": null,
  "error": {
    "code": "msg-1001",
    "message": "The source root /tmp/nowhere does not exist or is not a directory.",
    "param": "root",
    "hint": "Pass an existing directory with --root, or create one with `stratarc init /tmp/nowhere`."
  }
}
```

`ok` is true and `error` is null on success, and `data` then holds the command's result. For `sync`, `check`, `diff`, `prune`, `reconcile`, `validate`, `projects`, `gen-rules-digest`, `components`, `drift` and `workflows`, `data` holds `command`, `exit`, `stdout` and `stderr` whenever the command ran, whatever its status; a refusal before it runs, such as `msg-1001`, leaves `data` null. `exit` is the status stratarc exits with, after the drift mapping under [Exit Statuses](#exit-statuses), so `stratarc --json check` on a drifted deployment reports `"exit": 6`. Without `--json`, a refusal prints one line headed by its message id, one line of recovery and a link to the message's entry in [Errors](generated/errors.md) to standard error.

## Mistyped Commands and Arguments

An unknown command is refused with `msg-1010`, which names the closest command when one is near (`stratarc synk` suggests `stratarc sync`). An argument a command does not take is refused with `msg-1014`, after that command's own usage line, and its recovery names `stratarc help COMMAND`. The arguments are checked before the source root is looked for, so a mistyped option is reported as such in any directory. Both exit 2, and with `--json` both print one envelope like any other refusal.

## Exit Statuses

| status | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | failure: the command ran and did not succeed |
| 2 | invalid input: a bad argument, an unknown source root, an invalid `stratarc.toml`, or a refusal by the engine |
| 3 | denied: the home is missing or not writable |
| 4 | conflict: the target already holds something |
| 5 | unavailable: a packaged resource is missing, a file in the home is newer than this stratarc, an adapter does not support the installed runtime, or the change log database is locked |
| 6 | drift: the deployed files differ from what the source renders |
| 130 | interrupted |

A command that reports drift (`check`, `reconcile --check`, `projects --check`, `projects --verify`, `gen-rules-digest --check`, `drift`) exits 6 where its module returns 1.

| variable | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `STRATARC_SOURCE` | the source root |
| `STRATARC_HOME` | the directory the home and every `~` in a target resolve under |
| `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR` | the projects root |
| `STRATARC_NAME` | the name Stratarc puts on what it generates; see [Configuration](configuration.md) |
| `STRATARC_HELD_PROJECTS` | the projects this machine holds: unset or `all`, `present`, or a comma separated list of names |
| `STRATARC_LOG` | set to `1` to turn on the change log database |

# Configuration

This page documents `stratarc.toml`, the file in a source root that names the enabled runtimes, their target directories, the projects root, the source root's layout and the optional workflow module, together with the environment variables that override them and the JSON Schemas that validate the other files in a source root. The environment variables are also listed in [CLI](cli.md).

## Stratarc.toml

`stratarc init` writes this file at the root of the source root with every key present and commented. A missing file yields the defaults; a malformed one stops the command with a message naming the file.

| key | type | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | `"stratarc"` | the name put on what Stratarc generates: marker comments, permission profile names, the deploy stamp file and the MCP ledger; lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter |
| `projects_root` | string | `"~/projects"` | the directory that holds your project checkouts; `~` expands to your home directory |
| `validate.gate_private` | boolean | `false` | whether the deploy gate also runs the checks in `scripts/private/validate_checks.py`; false gates a deploy on the built-in checks only, true makes a failing or broken extra check block the sync and names the file |
| `runtimes.<name>.enabled` | boolean | `false` for a table that omits it; a runtime with no table is enabled | whether `sync`, `check`, `diff` and `prune` act on this runtime |
| `runtimes.<name>.target` | string | the runtime's conventional directory | the directory the runtime reads its configuration from; `~` expands to your home directory |
| `layout.project_config_dir` | string | `"projects-root"` | the directory in the source root that holds one folder of project configuration per project; `stratarc init` writes `"projects/roots"` |
| `layout.control_plane` | string | `"control-plane.md"` | the control plane file, relative to the source root; `stratarc init` writes `"projects/roots/control-plane.md"` |
| `layout.local_dir` | string | `".docs"` | the folder in each project checkout that holds internal work product; `stratarc init` writes `"local"` |
| `layout.control_plane_managed` | boolean | `true` | false marks the control plane as maintained by hand, and `reconcile` then leaves it and the project snapshots alone |
| `workflows` | table | absent, the module is off | the optional workflow module; see [The Workflows Table](#the-workflows-table) |

The `layout` values are relative paths inside their root and may not contain `..`. An unknown `layout` key is an error. The defaults in the table are what a source root with no `[layout]` table gets, which is the layout Stratarc 0.3 scaffolded; a source root `stratarc init` writes today names the `projects/roots` layout explicitly. Every guide in these docs names the project configuration directory and the control plane by these keys' values, so read `projects/roots/` and `projects/roots/control-plane.md` as `projects-root/` and `control-plane.md` in a 0.3 source root.

The recognised runtime names and their default targets are `claude` (`~/.claude`), `codex` (`~/.codex`), `gemini` (`~/.gemini`), `cursor` (`~/.cursor`) and `opencode` (`~/.config/opencode`), plus any runtime with an adapter in `adapters/` in the source root. A `runtimes` table whose name matches no adapter is an error. See [Runtimes](runtimes/README.md) for what each receives.
