`[workflows]` in `stratarc.toml` sets the control plane defaults of the optional workflow module, and a project overrides them in `<layout.project_config_dir>/<project>/workflows.toml`, table by table. The module is off unless a layer sets `enabled = true`. `stratarc workflows check` validates both layers and `stratarc workflows show` prints the effective configuration. An unknown key is a problem.

| key | values | default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` or `false` | `false` |
| `paths.plan`, `paths.handoff`, `paths.backlog`, `paths.reports` | non-empty strings | `PLAN.md`, `local/handoff.md`, `local/backlog.md`, `local/reports` |
| `claims.mode` | `plan`, `files` or `off` | `plan` |
| `gates.<action>` | `G0` to `G3`, never below the action's standing floor or, in a project, below the control plane's value | the floor: `local-edit` G0; `push-branch`, `open-pr`, `release-candidate` G1; `create-issue`, `merge-default-branch`, `deploy`, `publish`, `delete`, `external-repo-write` G2; `bypass-guard`, `settle-decision` G3 |
| `decision-records.enabled` | `true` or `false` | `false` |
| `decision-records.root`, `decision-records.index` | non-empty strings | `docs/decision-records`, `docs/decision-records/index.json` |
| `decision-records.domains` | list of non-empty strings | `architecture`, `content`, `design`, `data`, `integrations` |
| `decision-records.target-words` | positive integer | `300` |
| `decision-records.check` | `report`, `enforce` or `off` | `report` |
| `tickets.backend` | `github`, `backlog` or `off` | `backlog` |
| `automation.session-start`, `automation.session-stop`, `automation.ci` | `true` or `false` | `false` |
| `automation.pre-commit` | `report`, `enforce` or `off` | `report` |
| `automation.triage` | `on-demand`, `weekly` or `off` | `on-demand` |

## How Values Are Resolved

Everything is read when a command runs, never when the module is imported, so a flag or a test can redirect it.

| value | order |
| --- | --- |
| home | `STRATARC_HOME`, then `HOME`, then the platform home |
| source root | `--root`, then `STRATARC_SOURCE`, then the nearest directory at or above the current one that holds `stratarc.toml`, then `source_root` in `~/.stratarc/config.toml` when that directory still holds `stratarc.toml`, then the current directory; a command that reads the source refuses the current directory when it holds no `stratarc.toml` |
| projects root | `--projects-root`, then `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR`, then `projects_root` in `stratarc.toml`, then `~/projects` |
| name | `STRATARC_NAME`, then `name` in `stratarc.toml`, then `stratarc` |

## Environment Variables

| variable | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `STRATARC_HOME` | replaces the directory that `~` and the `.stratarc` home live under |
| `STRATARC_SOURCE` | the source root |
| `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR` | the projects root |
| `STRATARC_NAME` | the generated-name override |
| `STRATARC_HELD_PROJECTS` | the projects this machine holds, for a machine that has fewer checkouts than the shared control plane lists |
| `STRATARC_LOG` | `1` turns on the change log database; the human-readable log is always on |

## The Home Directory

Stratarc keeps machine state, not project state, in `~/.stratarc`: `config.toml` (settings such as `logging`, and `source_root`, the source root `stratarc setup` recorded), `adapters/` (registered adapter manifests), `state/` (including `deployed.json`, the deploy ledger `prune` reads), `backups/` (including `backups/prune/`, a copy of every file `prune` deleted, which `doctor --clean` keeps), `logs/` and `cache/`. Directories are mode 0700 and files 0600. A file written by a newer Stratarc is never rewritten by an older one. `stratarc doctor --clean` removes only old backups and the cache.

## Schemas

Three JSON Schemas ship with the package under `stratarc/data/schema/` and validate the JSON files in a source root.

| schema | validates |
| --- | --- |
| `hooks.schema.json` | `hooks/hooks.json`, the hook registry: each canonical event maps to a list of hook groups with an optional tool matcher and command hooks |
| `permissions.schema.json` | `permissions.json`, the single permission policy every runtime adapter translates |
| `components.schema.json` | `components.json`, the manifest of external components |

See [Source Layout](source-layout.md) for the keys of `permissions.json` and `components.json`.

# Control Plane

The control plane is the file `layout.control_plane` in `stratarc.toml` names: `projects/roots/control-plane.md` in a source root `stratarc init` writes, `control-plane.md` at the top of a 0.3 source root. It is a Markdown file made of tables, written by `stratarc reconcile` and read by every adapter and every project delivery, that records which source item reaches which scope. This page describes its format. For using it, see [Use the Control Plane](../how-to-guides/use-the-control-plane.md).

## Scopes

A scope is a column. The first is `global`, which stands for the user-level runtime directories (`~/.claude` and the rest). Every other column is a project, named like its checkout. A project gets a column when it has a checkout under the projects root and is not a public target.

## Tables

After the introduction, a `projects` table and a short `configuration` note, the file holds one table per kind of item. A table's heading is its kind, and its first column, `option`, holds a link to the source file whose text is the row id.

| table | row ids | one row per |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `instruction-file` | `AGENTS.md` | the instruction file |
| `rules` | `rule:<name>` | file in `rules/`; this table also has a `tier` column |
| `hooks-<event>` | `hook:<name>` | hook script registered for that event; an event with no script has no table |
| `skills` | `skill:<name>` | directory in `skills/` with a `SKILL.md` |
| `commands` | `command:<name>` | file in `commands/` |
| `agents` | `agent:<name>` | file in `agents/` |
| `mcp-servers`, `plugins` | `mcp:<name>`, `plugin:<name>` | wanted MCP server or plugin in `components.json`; absent until one is declared |
| `project-local-configuration` | `project:AGENTS.md`, `project:rules`, and so on | project-local item under the project configuration directory (`layout.project_config_dir`) |
| `runtimes` | `runtime:<name>` | adapter, shipped or in `adapters/` |

```markdown
## rules

| option | tier | global | notes-cli |
|---|---|---|---|
| [rule:never-commit-local-databases](rules/never-commit-local-databases.md) | global | x | x |
| [rule:conventional-commit-messages](rules/conventional-commit-messages.md) | common | x | x |
| [rule:tests-use-a-temporary-directory](rules/tests-use-a-temporary-directory.md) | project |  | x |
```

## Cells

An `x` in a cell opts the item in for that scope. Any other content, including an empty cell, opts it out. Reconcile never changes a cell that already exists. A new row gets its defaults:

| item | `global` | project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rule in the `global` tier | on | on |
| rule in the `common` tier | on | on |
| rule in the `project` tier | off | off |
| skill, command, agent, hook | on | off |
| MCP server, plugin | off | off |
| runtime | on | off |
| project-local item | off | on for its own project |

## The Projects Table

```markdown
| project | status | tier | template | origin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| notes-cli | active | normal | base | example-owner/notes-cli |
```

`status` comes from where the checkout sits: `active` for a checkout directly under the projects root or under `active/`, and the folder name (`new`, `inactive`, `archived`, `external`) otherwise. Only `active` projects receive configuration. `tier` is `low` for `archived` and `external` and `normal` for the rest. `origin` is the `owner/repo` of the checkout's `origin` remote when it is a GitHub URL.

## Per-Project Snapshots

Each active project also gets `<local_dir>/stratarc-control-plane.md` (`local/` in a new source root, `.docs/` when `layout.local_dir` is unset), a generated copy of its own column, so a session inside the project can read what it was given. Reconcile writes it only from the primary checkout of the source root, never from a linked worktree. The file is rewritten on every reconcile and is not meant to be edited.

## Staleness

`stratarc reconcile --check` exits 6 when the file differs from what reconcile would write. A sync, a diff and a check print `control-plane: stale` when they find it out of date, and a sync fixes it before it renders.

# Package Data

This page describes how the runtime assets under `stratarc/data/` are packaged and resolved, for a contributor adding an asset or changing code that reads one. The assets are the source-root template, the JSON Schemas and a few hook libraries. They are read through `importlib.resources`, never through a path built from `__file__` or relative to the repository root, so a checkout and an installed wheel behave identically.

## What Lives Under Data

| path | contents |
| --- | --- |
| `stratarc/data/templates/source-root/` | the tree `stratarc init` copies into a new source root |
| `stratarc/data/schema/` | `hooks.schema.json`, `permissions.schema.json`, `components.schema.json` and `adapter-manifest.schema.json`, with a README describing each |
| `stratarc/data/hooks/` | the OpenCode hook plugin, the empty default hook registry, the list of retired hook names, and `lib/`: the token-shaped value detector, a logging helper and the public-target reader |

## How Code Reaches an Asset

`stratarc/resources.py` exposes one function:

```python
from stratarc.resources import data_dir

template = data_dir("templates/source-root")
```

`data_dir` starts from `importlib.resources.files("stratarc") / "data"` and walks the slash-separated name one segment at a time, returning a `Traversable`. Callers use the `Traversable` interface (`iterdir`, `is_dir`, `is_file`, `read_bytes`) rather than converting it to a filesystem path, because in an installed package it may not be one. `stratarc/cli.py` copies the template that way: it iterates the `Traversable` and writes each file's bytes to the target, skipping `__pycache__`.

## How the Assets Ship

`pyproject.toml` builds with hatchling and lists `stratarc/data/**` under `artifacts` for both the wheel and the sdist. That line is what carries non-Python files, dotfiles included, into the distribution; without it only `.py` files would ship and `stratarc init` from an installed wheel would find no template. The sdist additionally includes `tests`, `examples`, `README.md`, `LICENSE` and `pyproject.toml`.

## How It Is Tested

`tests/test_wheel_install.py`, marked `slow`, builds a wheel from the checkout, installs it into a fresh virtual environment and runs the installed `stratarc init` with the working directory outside the checkout, so the installed package and not the source tree is imported. It compares the scaffold with the template byte for byte, runs a dry-run sync and `doctor` under a temporary `HOME`, and adds a runtime of its own with `adapter new`. `tests/test_cli.py` checks the same copy from the checkout. Together they catch an asset that was added to the tree but not to the distribution, and a reader that works only when `data/` is a real directory.

## Adding an Asset

1. Put the file under the right directory in `stratarc/data/`.
2. Reach it through `data_dir("<path under data>")` and the `Traversable` interface.
3. Run the full test suite including the slow test; see [Run the Tests](../how-to-guides/run-the-tests.md).

No change to `pyproject.toml` is needed: the `artifacts` glob already covers everything under `stratarc/data/`.

# Source Layout

This page describes the source root that `stratarc init` creates: each file and directory, what it holds, which runtimes read it and the keys of the two JSON files that have many. The bundled template under `stratarc/data/templates/source-root/` is the authority for the shape, and [examples/notes-cli](../../examples/notes-cli/README.md) shows a populated one.

## Files

| path | holds | read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | the instructions every agent session starts from, with a marked block where the rules digest is written | every runtime |
| `stratarc.toml` | the enabled runtimes, their targets, the projects root and the layout of this source root; see [Configuration](configuration.md) | Stratarc itself |
| `permissions.json` | the single permission policy, translated into each runtime's native allow, deny and ask lists | every runtime with a permission model |
| `components.json` | external components: MCP servers, plugins, foreign hook groups, third-party skills and dependencies | every runtime that supports the component |
| `projects/roots/control-plane.md` | generated tables of which item reaches which scope; see [Control Plane](control-plane.md) | Stratarc itself |
| `projects/roots/public-targets.json` | optional: repositories that must receive nothing; see [Set Up a Project](../how-to-guides/set-up-a-project.md) | Stratarc itself |
| `.github/workflows/drift.yml` | a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `stratarc drift --source` on the source root | GitHub Actions |

## Directories

| path | holds | format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rules/` | one Markdown file per standing rule, and `tiers.json` naming each rule's tier | an H1 equal to the filename stem and a `## binding` section |
| `hooks/` | `hooks.json`, the hook registry, and the scripts it names | [Add a Hook](../how-to-guides/add-a-hook.md) |
| `skills/` | one directory per skill | a `SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` frontmatter |
| `commands/` | one Markdown file per slash command | `description` frontmatter, optional `argument-hint` and `allowed-tools` |
| `agents/` | one Markdown file per subagent | `name` and `description` frontmatter, optional `tools` and `model` |
| `projects/roots/` | one directory per project holding its project-local configuration | [Set Up a Project](../how-to-guides/set-up-a-project.md) |
| `templates/project/` | what `stratarc projects --new NAME` copies for a new project: `roots/` into the project configuration directory, `checkout/` into the checkout | [Set Up a Project](../how-to-guides/set-up-a-project.md) |
| `adapters/` | one Python file per runtime of your own | [Adapter Files](adapter-files.md) |
| `scripts/private/` | optional extra validator checks and project renderers | `validate_checks.py` declares `VALIDATE_CHECKS`; `project_renderers.py` declares `register` |

The paths above are the layout `stratarc init` writes, named by the `[layout]` table in `stratarc.toml`. A source root made by Stratarc 0.3 has no `[layout]` table and keeps the control plane at `control-plane.md` and the project folders, `public-targets.json` included, in `projects-root/`; see [Configuration](configuration.md).

Each directory the template creates holds a `README.md` describing the files that belong in it. A `README.md` is documentation and is never treated as a rule, command or agent.

## Permissions.json

| key | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schemaVersion` | always `1` |
| `policyVersion` | an integer you raise when a change must not be undone by an older checkout; a deploy refuses to write a lower version over a higher one |
| `defaultMode` | the runtime's default permission mode; `default` asks, anything that suppresses prompts is passed through |
| `codexApprovalPolicy` | `on-request` or `never` |
| `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories` | passed to Claude Code's permissions object |
| `additionalDirectories` | directories outside the working directory the policy treats as yours |
| `runtimeDirectories` | the runtime configuration roots a sync may write into and that stay writable to agents; every enabled runtime's target must be listed |
| `codexNetwork` | `{"enabled": bool, "domains": {...}}` for Codex |
| `codexShellEnvironment` | `{"passthrough": [names]}`, the environment variables Codex passes to shell commands |
| `allow`, `deny`, `ask` | rule strings in Claude Code syntax, such as `Read(~/projects/**)`, `Bash(git status)` or `Edit(**/.env)` |
| `autoMode` | Claude Code's auto-mode guidance block, passed through whole |

## Components.json

A `version` of `1`, an optional `runtime_settings` object, and five sections, each a list of entries (or `null`):

| section | an entry declares |
| --- | --- |
| `mcp_servers` | an MCP server: `command` with `args`, `env` and `cwd`, or a `url` with `transport`, or `hosted: true` for a connector another account runs |
| `plugins` | a plugin: its `marketplace`, or a `path` for an OpenCode file plugin |
| `foreign_hooks` | a hook group another tool registers: the `match` text that finds it, and optionally a `registration` Stratarc renders |
| `third_party_skills` | skills another tool installs: its `installer`, and the directory names when one install makes several |
| `dependencies` | a command-line tool: `command`, `install`, a pinned `version`, and optionally `version_command` and `platform` |

Every entry carries `name`, `runtimes` (a list of runtime names), `owner` and `wanted`, and optionally `description`. An entry whose `owner` is the engine name (`stratarc` unless you changed it) is rendered into each listed runtime that supports it. Any other owner means another tool installs the component, so Stratarc only records that it is expected. `wanted: false` declares a component known and deliberately unwanted: `check` reports it as returned, and `prune` can remove it. A key an entry may not have is an error, and so is a literal that looks like a credential; write secrets as `secret://namespace/key`.

`runtime_settings.<runtime>` holds `model`, `subagent_model`, `aliases` (short names to the runtime's model names), `settings` (passed through into the runtime's own settings) and, for OpenCode, `provider`.

## Rules/tiers.json

```json
{
  "global": ["never-commit-local-databases.md"],
  "common": ["conventional-commit-messages.md"],
  "project": ["tests-use-a-temporary-directory.md"]
}
```

A rule that no tier names is not rendered. See [Add a Rule](../how-to-guides/add-a-rule.md).

# First Contribution

This tutorial takes you from a fresh clone to a change that is ready for review. You set up a development environment, run the test suite, make one small change and check it. It follows one path and explains only what that path needs; [Contributing](../../CONTRIBUTING.md) holds the guidelines it applies, and the [how-to guides](../how-to-guides/README.md) cover each step in more depth.

## What You Need

- Python 3.11 or newer.
- `git`, and a GitHub account if you intend to open a pull request.

## Clone and Install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/klappe-pm/stratarc ~/stratarc && cd ~/stratarc && python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[test]'
```

This installs Stratarc as an editable package with `pytest` and `jsonschema`, the only test dependencies. The command itself has no runtime dependencies.

## Run the Tests

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

The full suite includes one slow test that builds a wheel, installs it into a fresh virtual environment and checks that the installed command scaffolds a source root and syncs a runtime of your own. While iterating, skip it:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m 'not slow'
```

Run the full suite before you commit. See [Run the Tests](../how-to-guides/run-the-tests.md) for the other checks.

## Make a Change

Pick something small for a first change: a wording fix in a page under `docs/`, a missing edge case in `tests/`, a clearer message in `stratarc/messages.py`. Read the part of the user documentation that covers what you are changing first, and [Source Layout](../reference/source-layout.md) if the change touches the template.

Two conventions catch newcomers. Runtime assets under `stratarc/data/` are reached only through `importlib.resources`, never through a path built from `__file__`; see [Package Data](../reference/package-data.md) for why. And a user-facing message is added to the catalog in `stratarc/messages.py` first, then raised by id.

## Check It

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python -m pytest
```

If you changed a command, an option or a message, regenerate the two reference pages that come from the code and commit the result:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc && .venv/bin/python scripts/docs/generate-reference.py
```

## Commit

Commit with a [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) message, for example `docs: clarify the init target rule` or `fix: refuse an init target that is a file`. Add a line under Unreleased in [the changelog](../../CHANGELOG.md) if the change is visible to a user. Keep the change to one thing, and say in the pull request what it does and how you tested it.

## Next Steps

- Read [Architecture](../explanation/architecture.md) before a change that touches more than one part of the pipeline.
- Read [Add a Runtime](../how-to-guides/add-a-runtime.md) to see how a runtime of your own is added.
- Read the [decision records](../explanation/decisions/README.md) before proposing a change to something they settle.

# Getting Started

This tutorial takes you from an empty machine to a first deployment. You install the command, scaffold a source root, add one rule, preview the change and deploy it. It follows one path and explains only what that path needs. For every command see the [CLI reference](../reference/cli.md), and for every key in `stratarc.toml` see [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

## What You Need

- Python 3.11 or newer.
- `pipx`, or a virtual environment you are willing to install into.
- At least one supported runtime installed and run once, so its directory exists: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor or OpenCode.

## Install the Command

```bash
pipx install stratarc
```

```bash
stratarc --version
```

The [install guide](../how-to-guides/install.md) covers other install methods and upgrading.

## Run Setup

Run the command on its own:

```bash
stratarc
```

The first time, it starts a guided setup. It asks where your source root should live (press Enter for `~/stratarc-source`), writes the bundled template there, lists the runtimes it found installed and enables the ones you choose, then shows a preview of the first deploy. It deploys only if you answer `y`; answer `n` for now, since this tutorial adds a rule first. Setup records the source root in `~/.stratarc/config.toml`, so later commands find it from any directory, and running `stratarc` again prints where it is and what to run next.

If you would rather set things up by hand, or are working in a script, scaffold with `init` instead and edit the runtimes yourself, as the next two sections describe.

## Scaffold a Source Root by Hand

Pick a directory that does not exist yet, or is empty:

```bash
stratarc init ~/stratarc-source
```

`init` writes the bundled template: `AGENTS.md`, `stratarc.toml`, `permissions.json` and `components.json`; the `rules/`, `hooks/`, `skills/`, `commands/` and `agents/` directories, each with a short README that says what belongs in it; `projects/roots/`, which holds the control plane (`projects/roots/control-plane.md`) and one folder per project; `templates/project/`, the starting point for a new project; and `.github/workflows/drift.yml`, a workflow that reports drift. It refuses to write into a directory that already holds files. This directory is your source of truth. Put it in git.

The `[layout]` table in `stratarc.toml` names where the project folders and the control plane live. A source root made by Stratarc 0.3 has no such table and keeps them at `projects-root/` and `control-plane.md` instead; see [Configuration](../reference/configuration.md).

## Choose Your Runtimes by Hand

Setup already did this. Otherwise, open `~/stratarc-source/stratarc.toml`. There is one table per runtime. Set `enabled = true` for each runtime you use and leave the rest at `false`. A runtime is deployed to only when its directory already exists, so one you have not installed is skipped.

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync --list
```

The list shows each runtime and whether its target directory is present.

## Add a Rule

A rule is a short standing instruction. Create `~/stratarc-source/rules/greet-the-user.md`:

```markdown
# greet-the-user

## binding

Start each session by greeting the user by name.
```

List it in `~/stratarc-source/rules/tiers.json` so it is selected. The `global` tier applies everywhere:

```json
{
  "global": ["greet-the-user.md"],
  "common": [],
  "project": []
}
```

Tell Stratarc a source file was added:

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc reconcile
```

`reconcile` adds a row for the rule to `projects/roots/control-plane.md`, the table that records which items reach which scope. See [Use the Control Plane](../how-to-guides/use-the-control-plane.md) for how to read it.

## Preview the Change

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc diff
```

`diff` shows what a deployment would change in every enabled runtime and writes nothing. It runs `validate` first and refuses a source root with an error in it. `stratarc check` runs the same comparison and exits 6 when anything is out of date, which is what a script wants.

## Deploy

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc sync
```

`sync` renders the source into each enabled runtime. It writes only the files it owns and leaves everything else in a runtime directory alone. Open the runtime's instruction file, for example `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, and the rule is in the rules digest.

## Confirm and Recover

```bash
cd ~/stratarc-source && stratarc check
```

`check` now exits 0: everything deployed matches the source. To confirm a deploy as part of the write, and put the runtime files back if they do not match, use `stratarc sync --verify --rollback-on-drift`; [Roll Back a Deploy](../how-to-guides/roll-back-a-deploy.md) explains what that covers and how to restore a file by hand.

- Move an existing configuration in: [Migrate Existing Config](../how-to-guides/migrate-existing-config.md).
- Add skills, commands, agents and hooks: [Add a Skill, Command or Agent](../how-to-guides/add-a-skill-command-or-agent.md) and [Add a Hook](../how-to-guides/add-a-hook.md).

# Adapter Registry and Support Ranges

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09. Amended 2026-10-14: a source root can add adapters of its own, see [a runtime is one adapter file in the source root](2026-10-14-a-runtime-is-one-adapter-file-in-the-source-root.md).

## Context

Each adapter translates the source into one runtime's native files, and those runtimes change their formats. Deploying through an adapter that does not understand the installed runtime can write files the runtime rejects or misreads. The tool needs a way to say how far an adapter can be trusted and to retire one gracefully. See [registry.py](../../../stratarc/registry.py).

## Decision

Every adapter carries a manifest with a `supports` version range. Its status is `ok`, `outdated`, `unsupported` or `unknown`. An `unsupported` adapter blocks a deploy with exit 5, and an `outdated` one (newer than the version it was tested against) warns once per run. Deprecating an adapter prompts once and records the answer; a noninteractive run prints the notice and continues without recording. Bundled ranges are permissive until test fixtures record the runtime versions each adapter was built against. `stratarc adapter register` stores a manifest with a tighter range for an adapter that already exists; it never loads code.

## Alternatives

- No version checks. Simplest, but failures show up as broken runtime configuration.
- Block on `outdated` too. Safer, but it stops a deploy for a runtime that merely moved ahead of the tested version.
- Warn on every use. Noise teaches users to ignore it, so it is once per run.
- Narrow bundled ranges now. It would be a guess without recorded evidence.

## Consequences

- A hard mismatch stops before any file is written, with a recovery sentence.
- Permissive bundled ranges mean the gate protects registered manifests more than bundled ones until fixtures land.
- A deprecation answer recorded interactively spares scripts a prompt, and a script never hangs waiting for one.

# Diff Is a Read-Only Full Render

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

A user about to deploy wants to see what a sync would change before it changes anything. A summary that guessed at changes from file timestamps or a list of inputs could disagree with the real result, and a preview that wrote to the runtime directories would not be a preview.

## Decision

`stratarc diff`, and `sync --dry-run` without `--prune`, stage the source and run every adapter in check mode, which is the same render a sync performs, and print what would change. Deployed paths are shown with `~` for the home directory and never as staging paths, so the output is the same on every run. The command writes nothing and exits 0 even when it finds drift, because a diff reports a difference and is not a test. `stratarc check` is the command that gates: it exits 6 on drift. The flag handling is in [sync.py](../../../stratarc/sync.py) and the exit codes are listed in the [command reference](../../reference/cli.md).

## Alternatives

- Compare file timestamps or input hashes. Rejected: it can disagree with the real render and cannot show what a file would contain.
- Make `diff` exit non-zero on drift. Rejected: a script that only wants to read the preview would need to ignore the status, and `check` already gates.
- Combine `--dry-run` with `--prune` into the diff. Rejected: a prune lists what it would delete, which is a different report, so that pair keeps its own meaning and the combination of `--diff` with `--prune` is refused.

## Consequences

- The preview and the sync cannot drift apart, because they share the render.
- The cost of a diff is the cost of a full render, with no shortcut.
- Drift handling is split by command: `diff` reads, `check` decides, and a CI job that wants to fail on drift runs `check`.

# Exit Code Map

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

Scripts and CI jobs that call stratarc need to tell a bad argument from a refused write, a conflict, a missing prerequisite and a deployed file that no longer matches its source. A caller should be able to branch on the status alone, and read the same structured error when it asks for JSON.

## Decision

stratarc exits 0 for ok, 1 for failure, 2 for invalid input, 3 for denied, 4 for conflict, 5 for unavailable, 6 for drift or a failed verification and 130 for an interrupted run. With `--json` every command prints one JSON envelope, `{ok, data, error}`, where `error` carries `code`, `message`, `param` and `hint`. The codes live in [messages.py](../../../stratarc/messages.py) and are mapped to names in [cli.py](../../../stratarc/cli.py).

## Alternatives

- Exit 1 for every failure. Simple, but a script cannot tell a typo from a drifted deployment without parsing text.
- Reuse another tool's table unchanged. It lacks a code for drift and for a newer-schema refusal, so those would collapse into a generic failure.

## Consequences

- A script can branch on the status alone: 6 means rerun a sync, 5 means upgrade or wait, 2 means fix the call.
- A new failure class needs a new code only if callers must react differently to it; otherwise it reuses the nearest existing code.
- The numbers are part of the public contract and cannot be reassigned without a superseding record.

# Home Layout and Safe Writes

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

settled 2026-10-09 by [the home is `.stratarc`](2026-10-09-the-home-is-dot-stratarc-with-an-environment-override.md).

## Context

The tool keeps machine state (settings, adapter manifests, backups, logs, cache) apart from any project. That state is edited by commands and by hand, survives upgrades and can be written by a newer or older version of the tool. Losing or silently downgrading it would be costly. See [home_layout.py](../../../stratarc/home_layout.py).

## Decision

The `.stratarc` home holds `config.toml`, `adapters/`, `state/`, `backups/`, `logs/` and `cache/`. Directories are mode 0700 and files 0600, and every file carries a schema version. A file with a newer schema is never rewritten and the command exits 5. Every write first copies the file it replaces into `backups/`. A clean removes only backups and cache, and only with `--yes`; it keeps the newest 20 versions of each file plus anything under 30 days old.

## Alternatives

- Write in place with no backup. Simplest, but a bad write is unrecoverable.
- Silently migrate a newer file down. It would corrupt data written by a newer release.
- Let clean remove any state. It risks deleting user data such as registered adapter manifests, so only disposable directories are candidates.
- Use the XDG path only. Standard on some systems, but it splits the layout across platforms.

## Consequences

- A downgrade is safe: the old tool refuses to touch what it cannot understand.
- Backups grow until a clean runs, bounded by the keep rules.
- Secrets never live in the home; configuration refers to them by `secret://` reference.

# Message Catalog with IDs

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

Error wording scattered through the commands drifts: the same failure is described three ways, recovery advice is missing, and a document that quotes a message goes stale when the code changes. Users filing an issue also need a short stable handle for the message they saw.

## Decision

Every user-facing error has an id of the form `msg-NNNN`, one sentence that states the problem and one sentence that states the recovery, and the exit status it ends the command with. The catalog lives in [messages.py](../../../stratarc/messages.py), so wording is edited in one place and the documentation links to a message by its id instead of copying its text. A caller raises a message by id and fills its placeholders. Tracebacks appear only with `--debug`.

## Alternatives

- Inline strings at each raise site. Cheapest to write, but wording cannot be reviewed as a set and ids cannot exist.
- Message text in a data file. It would separate wording from code, but placeholders and exit statuses would then need their own validation and the catalog loses type checking.
- Always print tracebacks. Useful to maintainers, hostile to users who only need to know what to do next.

## Consequences

- Wording is reviewed and changed in one file, and a test can assert that every id has both sentences.
- Documentation survives a rewording because it cites the id.
- Adding an error means adding a catalog entry first, which is a small tax on every new failure path.
- Without `--debug` a maintainer sees less detail on an unexpected crash and must ask the reporter to rerun with it.

# Optional Change Log

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

Users want to ask what changed, when and why, and to verify a change later. Recording that costs disk, can capture sensitive text and can fail (a locked or newer database). The tool must never become unusable because its log is. See [changelog.py](../../../stratarc/changelog.py).

## Decision

A human-readable log is always on. The SQLite database and its JSONL mirror are off by default and turn on with `STRATARC_LOG`, `logging = true` in `config.toml`, or the `enable` command. The log stores digests, never content, and every text value passes the packaged token-shaped detector before it is written; if the detector cannot run, the value is replaced and nothing unredacted is written (it fails closed). A locked or newer database degrades to the human log with one message and never fails the command. Recording is a no-op while disabled and never fails a sync.

## Alternatives

- Always-on database. Richer history for everyone, but a write path, disk growth and a failure mode for users who never asked for them.
- A separate logging service. It would add a process to install, secure and keep running for what is a local file concern.
- Store the before and after content. It makes explanations easy but turns the log into a copy of the user's files and a leak risk.

## Consequences

- A fresh install writes only a plain text line per event, so the cost of the feature is opt in.
- Explaining a change relies on digests and the verify report, not on stored content, so it can say that something differed but not show the old bytes.
- A failing log can never block a deploy, at the price that an event may exist only in the human log and the mirror.

# Private Checks Gate Deploy Only When the Source Root Opts In

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09. Settles the open point in [private extensions live in the source root](2026-10-09-private-extensions-live-in-the-source-root.md).

## Context

A source root can load its own validator checks from `scripts/private/validate_checks.py`. The deploy gate runs the generic checks only, so a source root's own checks run under `stratarc validate` and never block a sync. A user who relies on their own checks to keep a deploy safe needs a way to make them block.

## Decision

The deploy gate runs the source root's private checks when `stratarc.toml` sets `[validate] gate_private = true`. The default is false, so a deploy depends only on the generic checks the package ships. A private check that raises or fails to load is an error finding, and under the gate it blocks the deploy with a message naming the file.

## Alternatives

Always gating on private checks was rejected because a stale or broken extension would block every sync for a reason outside the package. Never gating was rejected because it leaves a user's own safety checks advisory. A command-line flag only was rejected because the choice belongs to the source root and should not depend on who runs the sync.

## Consequences

A source root can turn its private checks into a gate with one line. The setting is part of `stratarc.toml`, so it is reviewed with the source it protects.

# Private Extensions Live in the Source Root

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

Some behavior belongs to one user's tree and not to the published engine: extra validation checks and renderers for particular projects. The engine needs a way to load these without containing them.

## Decision

Optional extensions live in the source root and are found through `paths.source_root()`. Extra validator checks are read from `scripts/private/validate_checks.py` ([validate.py](../../../stratarc/validate.py)), and project renderers from `scripts/private/project_renderers.py` ([projects.py](../../../stratarc/projects.py)). Each is loaded by file path. An absent extension is a no-op, and a broken one is reported and skipped so the rest of the run still completes. Runtimes are added the same way, from `adapters/`, see [a runtime is one adapter file in the source root](2026-10-14-a-runtime-is-one-adapter-file-in-the-source-root.md).

## Alternatives

- Python entry points. Rejected: a source root is not an installable package, so an entry point would force it to become one just to add a check.
- Configuration in `stratarc.toml` naming a module to import. Rejected: it adds a second place to look for something the source root's layout already locates.
- Build the extensions into the engine behind switches. Rejected: it would publish material that belongs to a single user and grow the engine for everyone.

## Consequences

- A source root with no extensions behaves as a plain one, with the generic checks only.
- Extensions are versioned with the source root that uses them, so they change in the same commit as the files they check.
- An extension runs arbitrary code from the source root, so loading one is a trust decision made by whoever owns that tree.
- A failing extension never loses the gate: the validator reports it as an error finding and keeps running the other checks.

# Projects Root from Config

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09. Amended 2026-10-14: the default is `<home>/projects` and checkouts may sit directly in it.

## Context

The engine delivers configuration into project checkouts and finds them under one directory. The location of that directory was settable only by a flag or an environment variable, and three modules each carried their own copy of the rule that locates it.

## Decision

`projects_root` in `stratarc.toml` feeds `paths.projects_root()`, and the precedence is the command line flag, then `STRATARC_PROJECTS_DIR`, then `stratarc.toml`, then the default `<home>/projects`. `paths.projects_dir()` returns that directory for every caller. Its children are either the checkouts themselves (a flat layout, where every checkout is active) or status folders (`active/`, `new/`, `inactive/`, `archived/`, `external/`) that hold them, so shelving a project means moving it to `archived/`. A checkout may also sit one grouping folder down. Both functions are in [paths.py](../../../stratarc/paths.py), and the config key is read by [config.py](../../../stratarc/config.py).

## Alternatives

- Keep the flag and the environment variable only. Rejected: a source root could not state where its projects live, so every user and every script had to repeat it.
- Require status folders. Rejected: most people keep checkouts in one flat directory, and a layout rule should not decide whether a project is found.
- Leave the three copies in place. Rejected: one function is a single place to test and to change.

## Consequences

- A source root carries its own projects location, so the same command works on any machine that shares it.
- An explicit flag still overrides everything, which keeps tests and one-off runs simple.
- The two functions take their arguments in different orders, which the docstring of `projects_dir` warns about.
- A flat root that also holds unrelated non-repository folders is fine: only directories with a `.git` entry are checkouts.

# Sync Records Changes at Its Write Points

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

The [change log](2026-10-09-optional-change-log.md) needs events to hold, and the sync engine is where nearly every write happens. The question was where to call the log, and what a logging failure may do to a sync.

## Decision

Sync records an event at each point where it changes something: the reconcile and project steps (one event per changed project), the plugin ingest declare and opt-in, the derived-file regeneration, each runtime after its adapter ran (status propagated, with a digest of the result and the shared cause id of the run), and the permission sweep. A refusal at any of those points records a failed event. Recording does nothing when logging is off, including the human log, and a failure to record or a locked database never stops a sync; the call degrades to the human log and prints one message.

## Alternatives

Recording from each adapter was rejected because adapters render and do not decide what counts as a change. Recording once at the end of a run was rejected because it loses which layer and which project each change reached. Failing the sync on a logging error was rejected because a diagnostic aid must not become a way to break a deploy.

## Consequences

The log reads as a causal chain from one source change to each runtime and project it reached. Any new write step in sync must add its own recording call, which a test over the call sites guards. The known cost is a few more lines at every write point.

# Sync Verifies and Rolls Back on Drift

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

A sync that writes files and exits 0 says only that the writes did not fail. It does not say that the deployed result equals what the source describes. The [verify](2026-10-09-verify-defines-drift-as-a-dry-run.md) command can answer that, and the [change log](2026-10-09-optional-change-log.md) can hold the answer next to the change that caused it. The open question was how much of this a single sync run should do on its own, and what a failed check may undo.

## Decision

`stratarc sync --verify` runs verification for the change it just made, using the shared cause id of the run, and records `verified` or `drift` in the log. `--rollback-on-drift` adds a restore: before the write the run backs up the files each adapter will change and each runtime's deploy stamp, and on drift it puts them back, removes files the run created and exits 6. If a backup is missing it exits 5 and says which. Rollback covers runtime targets and stamps only; project checkouts are verified but never rolled back. Both flags are refused together with `--only`, `--check`, `--diff`, `--dry-run`, `--prune` and `--list`.

## Alternatives

Verifying on every sync by default was rejected because it doubles the render cost for the common case. Rolling back project checkouts too was rejected because those are working trees that may hold uncommitted edits, and restoring over them could lose work. Leaving rollback to the user and the home backups was rejected because the backups exist to make the automatic path possible.

## Consequences

A run can promise that what is deployed matches the source, or that nothing changed. The cost is a second render when the flag is on. A drift in a project checkout is reported but left for the user to resolve, which keeps the working tree safe.

# The Home Is Dot Stratarc with an Environment Override

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09. Settles the open point in [home layout and safe writes](2026-10-09-home-layout-and-safe-writes.md).

## Context

The home layout record left open whether the XDG configuration path should be the primary home. The tool should install as a dot directory named after the product, and the code already resolves the home through one function.

## Decision

The home is `~/.stratarc`. `STRATARC_HOME` replaces the parent directory the dot directory lives in, which is how tests and containers redirect it. The tool does not read `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`. Source roots stay ordinary directories the user can commit anywhere.

## Alternatives

XDG as the primary home was rejected because one fixed location is easier to document, back up and find from an error message. Reading XDG only when set was rejected because two valid locations make every support question start with which one is in use.

## Consequences

The location is predictable on every platform. Users who keep dotfiles in XDG directories must set `STRATARC_HOME`. A later move to XDG would need a migration and a new record.

# Verify Defines Drift as a Dry Run

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

After a sync, a user needs to know whether what is deployed still matches what the source says. "Drift" can mean many things: a hand edit, a missing file, an extra file, a changed merge target. A vague definition produces false alarms, and a checker that writes to deployed files cannot be run safely from a script. See [verify.py](../../../stratarc/verify.py).

## Decision

`verify` re-renders the affected runtimes into a temporary stage through the same staging and adapters a sync uses, and compares the result with the deployed files byte for byte. It records `verified` or `drift` per file, never writes a deployed file and exits 6 on drift. Drift means exactly what an adapter's dry run would change. A stray file in a directory the tool does not manage is a matter for pruning, not drift.

## Alternatives

- Compare checksums recorded at the last sync. Cheap, but it misses a source change that was never deployed and trusts stale stamps.
- Treat any unexpected file as drift. Noisy: users keep their own files beside generated ones.
- Have verify repair what it finds. It would turn a read-only check into a write path with its own failure modes.

## Consequences

- Verify and sync agree by construction, because both use the adapters; a file reported as drift is one a sync would change.
- It is safe in CI and in the background, since it writes only its report and temporary files.
- Unmanaged extra files go unreported by verify and need the prune path.
- For a file an adapter merges into, the recorded digest of the render is not what a sync would leave; the report notes this.

# Version Detection Runs in an Isolated Home

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-09

## Context

The adapter registry learns each installed runtime's version by running its command with `--version`. The commands ran with the caller's full environment and working directory. Under a redirected home (the test suite, a container, or a user syncing against another home) the runtimes created their own directories and files inside it, such as `~/.codex/tmp/arg0`, `~/.cursor/cli-config.json`, `~/.gemini/projects.json.*.tmp` and `~/.config/opencode`. The next sync then saw those runtime targets as live and failed with `missing runtimeDirectories entry for ~/.<runtime>`. The same inheritance let the runtimes read the user's credentials and print credential notices, and a hung command could stall a sync for the old 10 second limit.

## Decision

`detect_versions` in [registry.py](../../../stratarc/registry.py) runs every detection command with these limits:

- `HOME`, the `XDG_*` base directories and the runtimes' own home variables point at a fresh temporary directory that is removed afterwards.
- The environment is an allowlist: `PATH`, `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TERM=dumb`, `NO_COLOR=1`, `CI=1` and the temporary homes. Tokens and every other variable are dropped.
- The working directory is the temporary directory, stdin is closed, and each command has a hard 5 second timeout.
- Any failure of one detection (missing command, timeout, non-zero exit, unparsable output, operating system error) gives an unknown version for that runtime and never raises.
- Results from the real runner are cached for the life of the process, keyed by runtime and resolved command path. An injected runner is never cached.

## Alternatives

- Keep the caller's environment and clean up afterwards. Rejected: it cannot undo a read of credentials, and a cleanup would delete files the user owned.
- Skip detection when the home is redirected. Rejected: the version is what the support range check needs, and a redirected home is a normal way to run.
- Parse the version from package metadata instead of running the command. Rejected: the runtimes ship in different forms, and only the command reports the version that will run.

## Consequences

- Detection cannot create files in, or read credentials from, the caller's home.
- A runtime that needs its configuration to print a version reports unknown instead. That is an allowed state of the registry and never blocks a sync.
- A repeated call in one process costs nothing, and a hung runtime costs at most 5 seconds.

# Rollback Places Every Adapter Action Line

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-10. Refines [sync verifies and rolls back on drift](2026-10-09-sync-verifies-and-rolls-back-on-drift.md), which stays as written.

## Context

`stratarc sync --rollback-on-drift` backed up only the files named by the adapters' dry-run action lines, and it found them by matching absolute paths under the runtime target. The claude adapter emits absolute paths. The codex, gemini and opencode adapters emit relative lines such as `copy commands/commit.md -> prompts/commit.md`, `translate commands/x.md`, `command x.md -> x.toml` and `render permissions.json into config.toml`, and some lines name no file at all (`map PreToolUse -> BeforeTool`, `trust 3 repositories in config.toml`). `verify._drifted_paths` returned those lines as unplaced and `sync._back_up_planned` discarded them. After a rollback those files stayed at the new content and files the run created were not removed. A study over redirected homes found it.

## Decision

`_drifted_paths` takes the set of files the adapter's render owns. A relative token counts as a file when it is an owned path or the tail of one. Without that set (the render failed), it places only the right side of `a -> b` and only when that side contains a slash, because a bare name could sit under any subdirectory.

Before a write, `_back_up_planned` renders the adapter into a throwaway directory and backs up every named path plus the whole owned set. A line that names no file is therefore covered by the set the adapter manages, not ignored. When the render fails and a line is still unplaced, the run records it, and the rollback refuses with msg-1119 (exit 5) instead of reporting a restore it cannot perform.

Tests: every runtime's dry-run lines are placeable against the owned set (all five runtimes), a full-tree snapshot of every runtime target is byte identical after a rolled-back run, and an unplaceable line refuses the rollback.

## Alternatives

Parsing each adapter's line format was rejected because the formats differ per adapter, several are not file paths, and any new adapter would break it silently. Treating the right side of every `->` as a target path was rejected because `map X -> Y` and `command x.md -> x.toml` would name files that do not exist. Snapshotting each whole runtime directory was rejected because the targets hold the user's own files, and the backups would copy all of them on every run. Ignoring unplaced lines was the defect.

## Consequences

A rollback backs up every file the render owns, not only those that change, so it copies more files than before for a run that rolls back or not. Rendering twice per runtime (once for the owned set, once to deploy) adds time to a rollback run only. Directories that a run creates (`mkdir hooks/...`) are not removed by the rollback, which restores and deletes files only, so an empty directory can remain. A file an adapter deletes outside its render and outside its dry-run lines is still not restored.

# Source Root Files Keep Their Mode and the Home Stays Private

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-10

## Context

`home_layout.safe_write` wrote every file with mode 0600, which suits the home (`~/.stratarc`) and is wrong for a source root. A source root is a user-visible directory that is often committed, shared with a team and read by other tools. A write that went through it silently turned a 0644 file into 0600, and a 0755 script into a non-executable one, while `stratarc init` wrote its files with the default 0644. The same tool therefore gave a source root two different modes depending on which command touched it.

## Decision

`safe_write` takes a `private` parameter that defaults to true. A private write keeps today's behavior: files 0600 and a missing parent directory 0700, with the missing ancestors inside the home made 0700 as well. A write with `private=False` is for a source root. The file keeps the mode of the file it replaces, a new file is 0644 and a missing parent directory is 0755, both subject to the umask, which matches `stratarc init`. An existing directory is never changed. The backup copy is 0600 in both cases because it lives in the home. The callers that write into a source root, such as the control-plane write and `adapter new`, pass `private=False`. Every other caller keeps the default.

## Alternatives

Making every write 0644 was rejected because the home holds state that should not be readable by other users. Reading a mode from the project configuration was rejected as more surface than the problem needs. Splitting the function in two was rejected because the backup, schema and atomic-replace logic is the same and would be duplicated. Changing `init` to 0600 was rejected because a scaffolded tree is meant to be committed and shared.

## Consequences

A source-root file is no longer changed in mode by an edit, so a committed file shows no mode change in a diff. The umask decides new files, as for any other tool that creates files. While writing the tests a second defect surfaced: when the first write into a fresh home was a backup, `.stratarc` itself was created with the default mode 0755 because only the leaf directory was changed to 0700. The ancestors inside the home are now changed too, and a test covers it.

# A Runtime Is One Adapter File in the Source Root

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-14

## Context

The promise of the tool is one configuration for any runtime, and five runtimes ship with it. A sixth runtime appears every few months, and a user should not have to wait for a release or fork the package to manage one. Before this record the registry listed only the adapters inside the package, so enabling `[runtimes.acme]` in `stratarc.toml` made `validate` and `sync` pass and write nothing.

## Decision

A runtime is one Python file, `adapters/<name>.py` in the source root, with the same contract as a packaged adapter: a literal `RUNTIME` dict naming the runtime, its target directory under the home, its hook registry file and the canonical hook events it handles, plus `sync(source, target, dry_run)` and `owned_outputs(source, target)`. The registry reads the `RUNTIME` constant of every file without importing it, then sync imports the file by path. `stratarc adapter new <name>` writes a working starting point and lists the new directory in `permissions.json`. The directory is read only when the source root has a `stratarc.toml`, so an unrelated `adapters/` folder is never treated as one.

Two refusals keep the failure loud. A `[runtimes.<name>]` table that no adapter provides stops `sync` and `validate --strict` with a message naming the missing file, and a source adapter that reuses a packaged runtime name is refused.

## Alternatives

- Python entry points. Rejected: a source root is a directory of configuration, not an installable package.
- A plugin directory in the home. Rejected: it would make the same source root behave differently on two machines.
- Registering a manifest only, as `adapter register` does. Rejected as the mechanism: it records version ranges for an adapter but loads nothing, so it cannot add a runtime.
- Silently ignoring an enabled runtime without an adapter. This was the defect.

## Consequences

- A new runtime travels with the source root and is reviewed in the same commit as the files it renders.
- A source adapter runs arbitrary Python at sync time, so owning the source root is a trust decision, the same as for private extensions.
- The runtime's directory must be listed in `permissions.json`, which `adapter new` does and `sync` enforces.

# Setup Remembers the Source Root in the Home

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-14. Adds one step to the source root precedence in [the home is dot stratarc](2026-10-09-the-home-is-dot-stratarc-with-an-environment-override.md) and uses the `config.toml` that [home layout and safe writes](2026-10-09-home-layout-and-safe-writes.md) defines.

## Context

A bare `stratarc` now starts a guided setup when it finds no source root, and prints a status summary when it finds one. The source root was found only through `--root`, `STRATARC_SOURCE`, or a `stratarc.toml` at or above the current directory, then the current directory itself. After setup, a user who runs `stratarc` from their home directory would find no source root and be sent through setup again. The fallback to the current directory also let `stratarc sync` run in any directory, where it wrote a `control-plane.md` before failing.

## Decision

`stratarc setup` records the chosen source root as `source_root` in `~/.stratarc/config.toml`, keeping every other key. The source root precedence becomes `--root`, `STRATARC_SOURCE`, the nearest `stratarc.toml` at or above the current directory, the remembered root when it still holds `stratarc.toml`, then the current directory. A command that reads the source refuses the current directory when it holds no `stratarc.toml` (`msg-1009`), so the last step only names the directory in an error. `stratarc doctor` names the step that decided and reports a remembered root that no longer holds `stratarc.toml` (`msg-1013`). Only `setup` writes the key; `init` stays a pure scaffold.

## Alternatives

Printing an `export STRATARC_SOURCE=...` line for the user to add to a shell profile needs no engine change, but a forgotten export sends the user back into setup, and the variable outranks a nearer `stratarc.toml`, which surprises anyone with a second source root. A fixed default location needs no record, but takes the choice of directory away from the user. Writing the key from `init` as well would make a scratch `init` in a test or a tutorial silently change which root every later command reads.

## Consequences

`stratarc` works from any directory after setup, and a source root checked out under the current directory still wins over the remembered one. A remembered root that is moved or deleted is skipped, not followed, and `doctor` says so. Tests must not read the developer's real home, so the test suite redirects the remembered file into each test's temporary home.

# The JSON Envelope Reports the Status Stratarc Exits With

## Status

accepted, 2026-10-14. Refines the envelope in [exit code map](2026-10-09-exit-code-map.md).

## Context

An engine command run with `--json` puts an `exit` field in `data`. It carried the status the command's module returned, before stratarc mapped it. A module that reports drift returns 1, which stratarc exits with as 6, so `stratarc --json check` printed `data.exit` 1 beside an error message that said "exited 6" and a process status of 6. A module status outside the exit code map, which stratarc exits with as 1, showed the same split. The field was not documented, so a caller had no way to know which number to trust.

## Decision

`data.exit` is the status stratarc exits with, after the drift and failure mapping. It always equals the process status and the number in a generated error message. The module's own return is not reported.

## Alternatives

Keeping the module's return under a second key, such as `module_exit`, would preserve a number no caller needs: the drift mapping is fixed by the command, so the module's return can be read off the documented table. Leaving `data.exit` as the module's return and rewording the message would keep the envelope disagreeing with the process status, which is the number scripts branch on.

## Consequences

A caller that read `data.exit` 1 as drift from `check`, `reconcile --check`, `projects --check`, `projects --verify` or `gen-rules-digest --check` must read 6. The field matches the `exit` of a `sync --verify` report, which already carried the mapped status. The change is listed under Changed in the CHANGELOG.

# Codex

This page is the reference for what Stratarc writes into the Codex target, `~/.codex/` by default. Codex reads different formats from Claude Code for permissions, commands and agents, so those are translated. The adapter is `stratarc/adapters/codex.py`.

## Target

`runtimes.codex.target` in `stratarc.toml`, default `~/.codex`.

## Outputs

| output | built from | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.md` with the rules digest | byte copy |
| `config.toml` | `permissions.json` | sets `approval_policy` from `codexApprovalPolicy` and `default_permissions` to the engine name, and writes a permission profile between `BEGIN` and `END` marker comments; the profile extends `:workspace`, lists the workspace roots, and denies the paths your `deny` list names |
| `config.toml` | `codexNetwork`, `codexShellEnvironment` | network access and the environment variables passed to shell commands |
| `config.toml` | `runtime_settings.codex` | `model` and `subagent_model` |
| `config.toml` | project checkouts under the projects root | each is marked trusted so Codex honours its project configuration |
| `config.toml` | `components.json` MCP servers | `[mcp_servers.<name>]` tables for the servers Stratarc owns |
| `rules/<name>.rules` | the `Bash(...)` entries of `allow`, `deny` and `ask` | `prefix_rule` lines: `allow`, `forbidden` for deny and `prompt` for ask |
| `hooks.json` | `hooks/hooks.json` | the same shape as Claude Code, with script paths pointing into `~/.codex/hooks` |
| `hooks/` | `hooks/*.sh` | executable bits kept |
| `skills/` | `skills/` | the `SKILL.md` format is the same |
| `prompts/` | `commands/*.md` | Codex calls a command a prompt |
| `agents/<name>.toml` | `agents/*.md` | a role file with `name`, `description`, `developer_instructions`, and a `model` mapped through the aliases |

## The Hook Plugin

`plugins/stratarc-hooks.ts` reads `hooks/hooks.json` and, for each OpenCode event, runs every command registered for the matching canonical event, with the payload on standard input in Claude Code's shape. OpenCode's lower-case tool names are mapped to the registry's (`bash` to `Bash`, `edit` and `write` to `Edit` and `Write`). A command that exits non-zero, or prints a JSON object with `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` set to `deny`, blocks the tool call with the reason it gives. A command whose script was not deployed exits 127 and is skipped, so a missing optional hook never blocks a call. `session.created` runs `SessionStart`, and a child session is a subagent: it runs `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop`.

`apply_patch` is matched as `Write` and checked once per affected file, so a hook that reads `tool_input.file_path` sees every path the patch touches: each added, updated and deleted file, and a move's destination as its own payload carrying `move_from`. Each payload also carries `operation` (`add`, `update` or `delete`), the lines the patch adds to that file as `content`, every parsed file as `files`, and the original patch as `patch_text`. Any one denial blocks the whole call. A patch the plugin cannot read (no file header, or a header it does not know) blocks before the call when a hook is registered for it, rather than being checked in part; after the call, the hooks receive it raw with a `parse_error`. The check sees what the patch says it will do; it cannot see files a hook script or the patch tool touches by other means.

The plugin runs inside OpenCode's own runtime and needs nothing extra installed. Other files in `plugins/` are yours and are never touched.

A database holds whatever the user typed into it, including text no one meant to publish. It also changes on every run, so it never produces a useful diff. Keeping databases out of version control is cheap; removing one from history later is not.

## binding
